#4838. Why So Many New Moms Are Told to Wait to Exercise Again—and What the Research Really Says

The six-week postpartum checkup was never meant to be about fitness.

Earlier this year, trainer and WH advisory board member Sohee Carpenter, CSCS, posted an Instagram Reel challenging some conventional postpartum advice: Don’t work out until your ob-gyn clears you at your six-week follow-up appointment. Her point wasn’t that new moms should rush back to the gym. It was that one timeline can’t fit everyone. Some women are ready to move sooner, and others need more time.

“I feel like so many people get angry because they assume we mean you're going to be doing a one-rep max back squat a week after you have a baby,” Carpenter says. “But that's definitely not what we're saying.” (By “we,” she means trainers who keep up with the latest research on pregnancy and postpartum exercise.)

The problem, Carpenter explains, is that the six-week rule isn’t based on evidence. On the contrary, research suggests that this type of blanket advice doesn’t make sense for something as personal as postpartum recovery. When you return to exercise after childbirth should depend on your own symptoms, not a date on the calendar.

“There's really nothing magical about the six-week time point,” says Margie Davenport, PhD, a professor of kinesiology at the University of Alberta and chair of the 2025 Canadian Guidelines for Physical Activity for Pregnancy and Postpartum—the first-ever exercise guidelines to specifically focus on evidence-based suggestions for that first year postpartum. In the U.S., the main guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) covers pregnancy and the postpartum period together. ACOG’s guidance points in the same direction, though: It says many women can start exercising again within days of an uncomplicated birth. In fact, “there is no identified ideal time to return,” Davenport says.

Based on the wide range of comments on Carpenter’s post—some supportive, some hypercritical, and still others asking more questions to try to better understand this shift away from the advice they’ve always heard—there’s still a lot of confusion around postpartum exercise. So we asked experts to break down what the research actually says, and how to approach working out in this new chapter of life.

In many cultures, the first 30 or 40 days postpartum is traditionally considered a protected time to rest, relax, and recover, Davenport says. In Chinese culture, it’s called zuo yuezi, which translates to “sitting the month.” In many Latin American and Latino communities, it’s known as “la cuarentena,” a nod to its roughly 40-day length. In South Korea, it’s sanhujori, or “postpartum care.”

These traditions carry deep cultural significance and are meant to offer real healing and support after birth from one’s community (they put “it takes a village” into practice). They’re rooted in caregiving and cultural custom, and they were never meant to serve as a medical timeline for when it’s safe to start exercising.

In Western medicine, six weeks has become an important medical benchmark in postpartum recovery—and, over time, a default point for returning to exercise too. “At that point, your uterus should be back to its pre-pregnancy state, and so a lot of the gynecologic changes should be fairly reversed by that point,” says Rita Deering, DPT, PhD, associate professor of exercise science and director of the Pelvic Health, Exercise & Musculoskeletal (PHEM) Research Laboratory at Marquette University.

The first six weeks after birth are also when the risk of complications like high blood pressure and infection is highest, Deering says, which is part of why that window became an important medical checkpoint (even though some pregnancy-related changes take longer to resolve). But, she says, “it was never intended to be about exercise.”

So how did six weeks become the exercise rule? Before researchers knew much about how safe it is to exercise during pregnancy and after birth, working out was considered potentially risky, Deering says. There wasn’t strong evidence that exercise wouldn’t slow healing or raise the odds of complications. So the most cautious advice was simply to wait until a doctor confirmed you’d healed enough to resume physical activity.

To come up with the 2025 Canadian Guidelines, researchers did a deep dive of all the available research on the topic, which included 574 unique studies organized into seven systematic reviews based on 21 different outcomes of postpartum exercise—such as depression and anxiety, low-back pain, injuries, glucose and blood pressure levels, and more. They also assembled an international panel of experts to give their recommendations.

Their advice: Start light-intensity physical activity and mobilization (think: carrying your baby around your home, a slow walk down the block, pelvic floor physical therapy) right away. From there, progress as you feel ready to moderate-to-vigorous activity such as brisk walking, resistance training, and running at your own pace—as long as tears and incisions have sufficiently healed and you don’t experience additional bleeding with exercise. (As mentioned, ACOG similarly recommends that women can return to postnatal exercise within days after an uncomplicated birth.)

Based on the research, there are no “absolute contraindications” to exercise postpartum, Davenport says—meaning no condition would rule out exercise entirely. There are some relative contraindications, she explains, “where you might have to delay a little bit or modify the type of activity that you're doing.” Examples include severe abdominal pain, extreme fatigue, and C-section incision pain that worsens with activity. All warrant a conversation with your doctor before starting.

Want to Know More About Lifting While Pregnant? Start Here

Pelvic floor symptoms, like leaking urine or a feeling of heaviness in the vagina, aren’t a reason to stop exercising altogether. If you notice signs of pelvic floor dysfunction, the guidelines recommend starting slowly and building up gradually instead. “Some leakage is okay,” Davenport says. “It means that the training that you’re doing is just overloading the muscle.”

Many people, including plenty of commenters on Carpenter’s Reel, worry that exercising after birth will damage the pelvic floor and cause dysfunction. But the evidence doesn’t support that. In fact, those muscles will likely be better off if you resume training, especially if you do exercises to target them in particular. “Engaging in pelvic floor muscle training reduces your risk of urinary incontinence by around 37 percent,” Davenport says. Additionally, if you stop all exercise because you're leaking a little bit, “this can actually mean that you're missing out on those other benefits.”

One caveat: If you’re leaking a lot, or it’s getting worse over time, “you probably need to pull it back,” Davenport says. That means being more selective about the moves you choose. For example, you might skip long runs and high-impact moves like jump squats for now, adds Sheridan Skye, a registered nurse, pre- and postnatal fitness coach, and founder of The Female Fitness Formula. Stick with lower-impact exercises, then build up gradually as you get stronger and your symptoms level off or improve.

At the end of the day, every body, birth, and recovery is vastly different. “Some people have a very uncomplicated labor and delivery and pregnancy; for others, it's quite complex,” says Davenport. “It only makes sense that the way that they're returning and what time they're actually returning is also going to be quite individualized.”

For some new moms, six weeks is too soon, and a blanket deadline only adds stress. “Maybe they aren't sleeping or they don't have the support to be able to return [to exercise] at six weeks,” Davenport says. On the flip side, for someone who had a straightforward delivery and is itching to get moving again, “telling them to wait for six weeks with no evidence to support it is also inappropriate.”

In fact, exercise can offer significant benefits during postpartum recovery, even before the six-week mark. “It improves muscle and bone density that we lose throughout pregnancy,” Skye says. Postpartum exercise is associated with a 45 percent reduction in the odds of developing postpartum depression, and starting before 12 weeks is even more beneficial.

It’s also associated with a 28 percent reduction in the risk of developing diabetes postpartum. Exercise even improves sleep quality, Skye notes. “Women tend to feel more energized and like they've experienced more rest, even if they haven't,” she says. (Anyone who’s survived a 3 a.m. feeding stretch knows that’s no small thing!)

There is also evidence that exercise in general can help to decrease pain, says Deering, and research links sedentary behavior to lumbopelvic (the areas of the lower back and pelvis) pain. “So if you are having pain, movement might be what you need to help with that.”

For many people, it may be difficult to know if you’re truly ready. “Especially when you're postpartum, it can feel like you are super out of touch with your body sensations, especially if you're not sleeping well,” Carpenter says.

If you're at the point where you're thinking about it, but are nervous or unsure or just overwhelmed by having another decision to make, Davenport recommends taking the Get Active Questionnaire for Postpartum—a tool that her team designed as part of the 2025 guideline. It can help you quickly understand if you’re ready to start from a medical perspective. That can help give you some reassurance.

There can also be “a lot of fear involved,” Carpenter says, especially if you had a C-section or are healing from a vaginal tear. In that case, “you’re probably going to be a bit hesitant,” which is completely understandable. Starting slower and lighter than you think you need to is perfectly fine as you get reacquainted with your body. “The first several sessions are really about mentally trying to get that confidence back,” she says.

As you go, pay attention to how your body responds. Leaking, for instance? That’s not a reason to stop exercising, but you may want to adjust your workout to reduce it. More bleeding, new pain, or a sense that something just doesn’t feel right are signs to stop, reassess, and possibly scale back. If they don’t improve, check in with your doctor. “It’s really about setting your ego aside and being willing to modify, even if it’s one rep to the next, based on how you’re feeling right at that time,” Carpenter says.

And if you feel physically ready but aren’t quite there mentally? “It’s okay to honor those feelings,” Deering says, “and to recognize that it’s okay to give yourself some time.” Whether that’s two weeks, six weeks, or six months, the right moment to start moving is the one that works for you.

She previously worked as deputy fitness editor at SELF, and is both an ACE-certified personal trainer and a ProNatal pre and postnatal fitness specialist. #4837. Before the Sell-Off, AI Stocks Showed Dot-Com-Level Bubble Signals: Study

Before the Sell-Off, AI Stocks Showed Dot-Com-Level Bubble Signals: Study

Researchers from London Business School and the University of Cambridge have estimated that there was as much as a 97% probability that AI-related stocks were in a financial bubble in September, before the recent sell-off wiped trillions of dollars off technology stocks.

The findings, highlighted Wednesday by London Business School, come from an analysis of 170 years of financial journalism. The researchers used artificial intelligence to determine whether the language journalists use to describe financial markets can help identify speculative bubbles before they burst.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short ANT with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

September's readings were comparable to or higher than those recorded at the peak of the dot-com bubble in March 2000, after which the Nasdaq lost roughly 77% of its value.

The research, titled Crying Wolf, was conducted by London Business School finance professor Marco Grotteria and Cambridge researchers Afonso Monteiro and Constantine Yannelis.

The team analyzed 795,964 articles published by The Economist between 1843 and 2013, identifying approximately 486,000 relevant to financial markets. They subsequently extended their index through September 2026.

Instead of simply counting how many times journalists mentioned the word "bubble," the researchers used large language models to identify language associated with excessive speculation, concerns about asset valuations, regulatory warnings, and investor euphoria. They then compared their monthly readings against 22 documented financial bubbles across 10 countries.

One of the more interesting findings was just how frequently financial journalists get it wrong. Historically, their coverage implied an average 20% probability of a major market crash within six months, compared with an actual frequency of just 5.7%.

What proved useful was measuring how much more concerned journalists became relative to their usual coverage. In 74% of comparisons between months during financial bubbles and ordinary months, the researchers' index registered a higher reading during the bubble, rising to 94% for the dot-com episode.

But the widely cited 97% figure represents the most pessimistic of the researchers' estimates. Two alternative calculations put the probability at approximately 40%.

The index also proved useful in forecasting stock market performance. When tested against data outside its estimation sample, it reduced the average squared error of 12-month Nasdaq return forecasts by 11% compared with predictions based on historical average returns.

Nvidia shares had fallen approximately 48% from their peak by last week, while the Nasdaq is trading well below its October record, prompting some analysts to raise concerns of a bubble.

Owen Lamont, a portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management and former University of Chicago finance professor who previously expressed skepticism about the existence of an AI bubble, has also revised his assessment, recently assigning a 70% probability to the U.S. stock market being in one.

The researchers distinguish between the economic potential of artificial intelligence and the amount of money investors expect to make from it. The internet fundamentally changed the global economy, for example, even though many of the companies that attracted enormous investments during the dot-com boom never survived its collapse.

"The technology may be very productive, but investors are still learning what it is worth," Marco Grotteria, one of the researchers said.

The study also found that central banks and regulators could reduce their expected losses by between 20% and 33% by incorporating the index into their decisions, provided they consider failing to identify a bubble substantially more damaging than issuing a false alarm.

For policymakers who assign equal costs to both mistakes, the researchers found no benefit from using the index.

#4836. Scout Motors starts validation builds at $2B SC plant, deliveries in 2028

Volkswagen’s revived Scout brand finally has vehicles coming off the line in South Carolina, but they’re validation units, not customer cars. Scout confirms the first deliveries of the Traveler SUV and Terra pickup won’t happen until 2028.

That’s two years later than the 2026 production start the company was talking about before it even broke ground on its $2 billion factory.

According to Scout’s announcement dated November 12, construction at the Production Center north of Columbia is in its final phase and most of the manufacturing equipment is installed. The Body Shop, Paint Shop, and Assembly Shop are all being used for the first validation builds.

The Body Shop is the most automated part of the plant. Scout says more than 750 robots join roughly 160 parts into each body, laying down about 5,000 weld points per vehicle, with AI-supported weld monitoring and a metrology system checking the results. At full capacity, the shop is designed to handle about 40 vehicles per hour.

Bodies then go through an electrified paint shop before landing in final assembly, where they’re married to the chassis and get their wiring, glass, seats, and wheels.

CEO Scott Keogh is clearly happy to have something physical to point to, saying that “what we are building in Blythewood is no longer a promise on paper.”

Scout also shared photos of a Terra pickup and a Traveler parked inside the plant. Its own fine print notes that they show “concept and validation vehicles” with optional features, so don’t read too much into what’s on display:

Fair enough. But Scout is also careful about what this stage is. Teams are confirming the equipment is installed and works, and checking engineering, buildability, and parts maturity. Process validation and scaling up to production speed come later. Validation builds will continue “into 2027,” followed by pre-production builds, and then customer deliveries in 2028.

The company says the plant will create more than 4,000 jobs, and it’s spending another $300 million on an onsite supplier park expected to support about 1,000 supplier jobs.

When Keogh laid out the plan in late 2023, Scout said it would start production in 2026 with deliveries shortly after. That was still the target when Scout broke ground in Blythewood in February 2024.

By the Traveler and Terra unveiling in October 2024, production had moved to 2027. Keogh then said in March that he expects the first customer to get a vehicle “sometime in 2028,” and that’s now the official line in Scout’s own press materials.

It might not even be the end of it. Industry forecaster AutoForecast Solutions has the Traveler starting production in September 2028 and the Terra in March 2030. Scout hasn’t confirmed those dates, but it hasn’t given more precise ones either.

The product itself has also changed under the hood. Scout launched as a pure EV brand, then added the “Harvester” range-extender option at the reveal. According to Keogh, Scout has more than 160,000 reservations, and 87% of them are for the gas-generator version. Those are $100 refundable reservations, not orders.

Der Spiegel reported earlier this year that integrating the range extender, which wasn’t part of the original plan, was among the technical problems pushing the timeline back.

For comparison, Tesla unveiled the Cybertruck in November 2019 and delivered the first ones four years later, a delay that was widely mocked. Scout is now on a similar four-year path from reveal to customer, and that’s for the SUV it’s launching first.

A working body shop with 750 robots isn’t vaporware. Scout has a real factory, a real workforce, and two vehicles that people clearly want. 160,000 reservations is a big number for a brand that hasn’t sold a single vehicle in 46 years.

But validation builds are an early step, not a finish line. Scout still has to go through pre-production, prove its processes, and ramp to rate, and every one of those stages is where new automakers usually lose time. Rivian and Lucid both learned that the hard way.

September 28? So we're 23 months away? I'm surprised the validation build yadda yadda stuff is supposed to take so long. It's not like VW doesn't know how to do this stuff, and that's a lot of money and equipment to sit mostly idle while 180,000 reservations holders are waiting for their cars. Maybe they're waiting for the market to change or are considering a whole other brand or product line?

And the market Scout was designed for in 2022 no longer exists. The EV tax credit is gone, and most of Scout’s own reservation holders picked the gas generator. In the US, the range-extender market is still early, unlike in China, where they are already popular.

But by 2028, Ford, Ram, and Jeep all plan to have range-extended trucks and SUVs on sale. Scout’s main advantage was being early with a cool, rugged, American-built electric truck. That advantage shrinks every quarter.

We’re still rooting for these vehicles. The Traveler and Terra are among the best-looking designs in the segment. But a $100 reservation is easy to walk away from, and the question is how many of those 160,000 people are still waiting in 2028.

#4834. Spain moves to grant financial watchdog power to freeze crypto accounts

A new decree would allow Spain’s financial intelligence unit to suspend crypto accounts, with firms facing fines for noncompliance.

A decree published on Nov. 25 would give Spain’s financial intelligence unit, Sepblac, the power to freeze crypto accounts and halt transactions without prior judicial authorization when it suspects money laundering or terrorist financing.

The measures are scheduled to take effect on Jan. 25, 2027. Under Spain’s Constitution, the Congress of Deputies must vote to ratify or repeal the decree within 30 days of its promulgation. If ratified, crypto companies operating in Spain would have to comply with suspension orders or face financial penalties.

According to the decree, Sepblac would be able to suspend the use of a digital asset account or a business relationship for up to five business days, while transactions in progress could be held for up to 10 business days. Although the initial suspension of an account or transaction would be at the discretion of Sepblac, it could be extended by a court at the request of public prosecutors.

Nikolai Timofejev, head of licensing and regulatory affairs at legal consulting firm Prifinance, told Cointelegraph that crypto firms should start preparing for the change before it takes effect. “My advice is to treat it like an operational workstream with a named person who receives Sepblac’s orders,” he said. “Non-compliance amounts to a very serious infringement attracting fines starting at €150,000.”

Timofejev explained that crypto companies should be ready to respond quickly, acting on suspension orders the day they receive them to avoid penalties.

The person in charge of responding to Sepblac’s orders should have the authority to “immediately (same day) freeze client withdrawals and transactions.” Companies affected would be responsible for tracking when each order expires.

Firms are also required to report suspicious activity to Sepblac, which, under the decree, would have three business days to issue a transaction suspension order if warranted.

Timofejev expressed support for the decree, saying he hoped “to see similar measures implemented across the entire EU.”

For crypto service providers operating in Spain, the new rules would add another layer of compliance obligations alongside those established under the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA).

#4833. What Is Self-Custody? How to Hold Your Own Crypto Keys

What Is Self-Custody? How to Hold Your Own Crypto Keys

When you buy crypto on an exchange, the exchange usually holds it for you. Your account shows a balance, but the private keys that control the coins belong to the trading platform.

The risk is that if an exchange collapses, is hacked or freezes withdrawals, its customers can lose access to their funds. The collapse of FTX in November 2022 left millions of users unable to withdraw, and turned the old crypto saying "not your keys, not your coins" into a rallying cry.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Self-custody is the alternative: holding your crypto yourself, with no intermediary standing between you and your money. This guide explains what self-custody is, how it works, the tools available and the risks it brings.

Self-custody means you, and only you, control the private keys to your crypto.

On a blockchain, coins are not stored in a wallet in the way cash sits in a purse. They are recorded on a public ledger, and a private key, a long secret number, is what proves you have the right to spend them. Whoever holds the private key controls the coins.

With a custodial service, such as a centralized exchange, the company holds the keys on your behalf, and you rely on it to process your withdrawals. With a self-custodial, or non-custodial, wallet, the keys are generated and stored on your own device, and transactions only happen when you approve them.

When you set up a self-custodial wallet, it generates a seed phrase, usually a list of 12 or 24 words. The seed phrase is a human-readable backup of your private keys: anyone who has it can recreate your wallet on another device and move your funds.

That makes the seed phrase the single most important thing to protect. Most guides recommend writing it down on paper or stamping it into metal, storing it somewhere safe offline, and never typing it into a website, sharing it or saving it in a photo or cloud file.

Self-custodial wallets come in several forms:

Custodial services are easier to use. If you forget your password, you can reset it, and an exchange handles the security of its own systems. But you are trusting the company to stay solvent, keep your funds safe and let you withdraw when you want to.

Self-custody removes that counterparty risk, and means no company can freeze your funds or block a transaction. The tradeoff is responsibility: there is no password reset. If you lose your seed phrase, or someone steals it, there is usually no way to get your crypto back.

Welshman James Howells says the keys to about 8,000 BTC are on a hard drive that was thrown out in 2013 and buried in a landfill in Newport, Wales.

Losing your keys is the most common risk, but not the only one.

Hardware can have flaws. In July 2026, a firmware vulnerability in Coldcard, a Bitcoin-only air-gapped hardware wallet, let attackers reconstruct some users' seed phrases. Losses rose to nearly $114 million in Bitcoin within days, according to Galaxy Research. Even the most secure devices depend on their makers getting the code right.

Phishing and malware are a constant threat to software wallets, and scammers often pose as wallet support staff to trick users into handing over seed phrases.

Holders also face physical danger. So-called "wrench attacks," in which criminals use violence to force victims to hand over crypto, have surged. Blockchain security firm CertiK verified 52 wrench attacks worldwide in the first half of 2026, up from 39 a year earlier, and Chainalysis said such attacks were on pace for a record year.

The threat is one reason holders have pushed back against proposals to make them report large self-custody holdings to tax authorities, warning that such records could leak.

Moving crypto off an exchange generally involves a few steps:

Regulators have long debated how to handle self-custodial, or "unhosted," wallets. In October 2026, the U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network withdrew a 2020 proposal that would have required banks and money services businesses to keep records on transactions with self-custodial wallets over $3,000 and report those over $10,000.

In France, the Senate rejected a plan in November 2026 that would have required holders to declare self-custodied crypto worth more than €100,000.

Self-custody is starting to extend beyond humans. In 2026, MetaMask launched Agent Wallet, a self-custodial wallet that lets AI agents execute on-chain trades within limits set by the user, while Coinbase introduced its own self-custodial wallets for AI agents.

Wallet makers are also working to make self-custody easier for newcomers, with features such as social logins and passkeys that reduce reliance on seed phrases. But the core principle remains the same: whoever controls the keys controls the crypto.

#4832. Japan weighs tighter oversight of DeFi, self-custodial wallets

Japan’s financial regulator is exploring measures to curb illicit finance risks, including potential restrictions on access to DeFi services.

Japan’s Financial Services Agency (FSA) is weighing potential new regulations for decentralized finance (DeFi) and self-custodial wallet providers as part of a broader effort to address risks associated with onchain finance.

In a discussion paper dated Thursday, the regulator raised the possibility of discouraging users from accessing DeFi services that lack adequate Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing controls.

The FSA also asked whether regulated businesses that interact with DeFi, including stablecoin issuers, on- and off-ramp providers and financial institutions, should play a role in mitigating illicit finance risks when no party responsible for regulatory compliance can be identified.

The regulator questioned how to identify parties responsible for DeFi services that claim to be decentralized but retain centralized elements, and whether front-end providers that give users access to decentralized exchanges should be subject to financial regulation.

The question of who should be held responsible for DeFi activities remains unresolved in other major markets. The European Union excludes fully decentralized crypto services without intermediaries from its Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation, while US regulators have largely focused on the nature of financial activities and the degree of control exercised by developers or operators. The stalled US CLARITY Act seeks to clarify which DeFi participants should be subject to financial regulation.

The FSA noted that direct regulation of self-custodial wallet use and providers that solely develop or sell software or hardware remains uncommon internationally but raised questions about whether additional measures are needed to protect users and prevent illicit financial activity.

Japan already requires domestic virtual asset service providers to collect information and maintain records on transactions involving self-custodial wallets, according to the FSA. Potential anti-fraud measures also include cooling-off periods for transfers from newly opened crypto exchange accounts to self-custodial wallets.

The discussions form part of a broader financial strategy announced by the FSA in July to promote onchain finance, with the initiative’s interim findings targeted for early 2027.

#4831. Waymo halts highway operation nationwide after CA DMV pause

Waymo has pulled its vehicles from highways nationwide after the California Department of Motor Vehicles ordered the company to pause highway operation in the state, following a viral video showing a Waymo trying to pass a police blockade.

Waymo is Google’s robotaxi subsidiary, which has been operating autonomously on public roads in some form since 2017. It has now expanded to 15 areas, recently adding another 250 square miles just last month.

The vehicles can be hailed through Waymo’s app, and operate with no driver in the driver’s seat, 24/7 in the covered areas. Since it can operate at any time but only within geofenced areas, this counts as “level 4” autonomy, as compared to the level 2 autonomy available on most consumer vehicles.

Until recently, Waymo only operated on city streets. These are more complex than highways, but lower speed. Accidents are more common on city streets than on highways, but can be more spectacular on highways given the higher speeds involved.

Most driver assist systems have been rolled out gradually, starting with highways, due to this lower complexity. But Waymo started with city streets first, bucking that trend.

The company started offering rides on highways late last year, but only in limited markets. It had been testing highway operation for several years prior, typically with a driver and with no public ridership.

Everything was going pretty well, with Waymo declaring its autonomous vehicles have stopped 841 injuries over the course of their 271 million miles of operation. And in terms of competition, Waymo is far ahead of Tesla’s Robotaxi effort.

But then, the viral internet stepped in. Last week, a video surfaced showing a Waymo trying to pass two police cars who were trying to slow down traffic on I-280 in Northern California. This is one of the main routes through Silicon Valley, and the opening of highway operations drastically reduced ride times in the area.

The video shows two police cars behind a construction vehicle, lights on and spread out across the freeway. Then it pans to show a Waymo vehicle moving quickly in the far left lane. One of the officers accelerates and swerves in front of the Waymo vehicle, at which point the Waymo swerves and slows down. (One media citation says that the video seems to have been sped up by the original poster, but we’ve embedded the short local news report on it above).

In response to this, the California DMV contacted Waymo and ordered the company to pause highway operations while it examines the incident. The order was made on November 11, but wasn’t reported until today.

The DMV cited multiple instances of Waymo vehicles incurring into construction zones, not simply the one viral clip above. It said that previous incidents had occurred and been noted, and corrective actions were implemented, but that the incidents keep happening.

This is a very rare situation which Waymo handled poorly. Waymo will add this case to their their test suite. They'll probably ask the CHP for their in car videos of other cases and convert those to be additional test cases. Waymo has been very willing to admit when their vehicles make mistakes in rare situations and fix it so that it doesn't happen again.

Waymo's vehicles are compared against perfect driving and Waymo accepts that as an aspirational goal. I note Tesla lacks the confidence in their system to even apply for the California permit to begin autonomous testing.

DMV’s pause will remain until Waymo can demonstrate “effective corrective actions” have been taken.

While the DMV’s order only applies to California highways, Waymo also paused highway operations in other states. It remains operating on city streets in all coverage areas.

Update: Waymo emailed us this statement after it saw this article

“Safety is at the foundation of everything we do. Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”

lululemon Hotty Hot High-Rise Lined Short

#4828. Hyundai reveals new 7-seat Neira electric SUV

Hyundai revealed the production-ready Neira EV for the first time, a three-row, seven-seat electric SUV set to launch in Indonesia on November 20.

After introducing the Neira Concept at the 2026 Gaikindo Indonesia International Auto Show (GIIAS) in July, Hyundai is gearing up to open pre-orders on November 20.

The Neira is a pretty “big” deal as Hyundai’s first locally produced seven-seat electric SUV in Indonesia.

Ahead of its official debut on Friday at GAIKINDO Auto Week (GAW) 2026, Hyundai offered a closer look at the upcoming Neira.

The electric SUV is essentially a Hyundai-badged version of the Kia Carens Clavis EV that launched last year. Aside from the Hyundai logos, a few minor tweaks to the front and rear ends, and new wheels and headlights, it’s a near replica.

Inside, both are equipped with dual 12.3″ instrument display and center navigation screens, plus an added climate control panel.

Hyundai didn’t reveal battery or powertrain specs, but the Neira is expected to use the same 42 kWh and 51.4 kWh battery packs as the Carens Clavis EV. The former offers an MIDC range of up to 251 mi (404 km), while the latter has up to 304 mi (490 km) on a single charge.

Both batteries can be charged from 10% to 80% in around 39 minutes using a 100 kW DC fast charger.

The Kia Carens Clavis is 4,550 mm long, 1,800 mm wide, and 1,708 mm tall, with a 2,780 mm wheelbase, so Hyundai’s Neira will likely be about the same size, if not slightly bigger.

Hyundai said the Neira has four key advantages: A higher ground clearance, Hyundai Bluelink connectivity tech, a Blind-spot View Monitor (BVM), and easy third-row access.

A post shared by Hyundai Motors Indonesia (@hyundaimotorindonesia)

Ahead of its upcoming launch, Hyundai is taking the electric 7-seater on a trip to prove its capabilities, going from Kilometer Nol in Banda Aceh to Banda Neira, which is about 4,000 kilometers (about 2,500 miles).

While Hyundai may export the Neira EV to overseas markets like India, don’t expect it to reach the US.

Hyundai already sells a three-row, seven-seat electric SUV, the IONIQ 9, which is built at Hyundai’s Metaplant in Georgia.

#4827. Ginger Rogers at Home: 10 Photos of the Golden Age Icon’s Glamorous SoCal Life

While most people race to the hospital to give birth, Ginger Rogers’s mother, Lela, insisted that her baby girl’s first breaths be taken in their Missouri home. “The little four-room house at 100 Moore Street was the perfect choice” for the future icon’s July 1911 welcome to the world, Rogers concluded in her 1991 memoir, Ginger: My Story. The star would go on to live with her extended family in Kansas City at 3306 Bellefountain Street; with her stepfather in Fort Worth at 1510 Cooper Street; and once she became a Hollywood sensation, a sprawling Beverly Hills estate. That joy and sense of peace she found in her childhood residence became a defining feature of her California pad. “It was a fun house, a happy house,” Rogers told Architectural Digest in 1994. “I was never angry when I didn’t have to work, because I liked to stay home so much.”

Decades after her death in 1995, Rogers is poised to return to the big screen by way of Sabrina Carpenter, who’s set to portray the late actor in the forthcoming, yet-to-be-titled Fred Astaire biopic. Tom Holland will star as Astaire. Read on for a glimpse inside the Oscar winner’s off-set life in the places she cherished most.

After Rogers separated from her second husband, actor Lew Ayres, in 1936, she and her mother moved in together. “I asked Mother if she would like me to build her a house, and if she did, could I live in it with her,” Rogers wrote in her memoir. “The next day she scoured the area for a suitable place to build. She found a wonderful lot high in Beverly Hills on 2.75 acres on Gilcrest Drive in Coldwater Canyon. It had a view that didn’t stop; when the fog burned off late every afternoon, it was possible to see Catalina.” Rogers is pictured at the stunning estate in this 1938 photo.

The actor with her home ice cream fountain.

The Swing Time star added many personal touches to the home, one of which was an elaborate soda fountain. In this 1940 photo, she’s shown whipping up a sweet treat. In her memoir, Rogers recalled all the amenities she installed. “The building took over a year because of labor strikes and material shortages,” she wrote. “When the house was finished, it proved to have been worth waiting for. It had everything I wanted or needed in a house: swimming pool, tennis court, projection room, and my very own soda fountain. Who could ask for anything more?”

Rogers opened her home tennis court to championship hopefuls so they could get practice matches in.

Rogers was an avid tennis player. Though she’s pictured here in 1950 at her Malibu beach house, the actor also had a home court installed at Gilcrest Drive. “On the way to the pool and tennis court were eight sculptured bay leaf trees. Next to the blue-tiled pool was my tennis court. This was my pride and joy,” she wrote in Ginger: My Story. With the knowledge that Rogers had the only en-tout-cas court in the area, the Tennis Association “begged” her to invite young hopefuls for some practice before they went on to championship matches at Forest Hills, New York. “I was delighted to open my court to competitors like Pancho Gonzales, Gussie Moran; and, later, Billie Jean King, Jennifer Hood, and Alice Marble slammed a few over the net too,” Rogers said.

Rogers was known for hosting her Hollywood star friends at home in Beverly Hills.

The Top Hat actor’s Beverly Hills abode was also a hot party spot for Rogers’s A-list friends. “My home was made for entertaining and I gave party after party,” she wrote in her memoir. “Most of them were informal. I’d serve spaghetti and we’d play some night tennis. Alcohol was never served, just cold drinks. One, a mixture of finely crushed ice, 7-Up, and concentrated orange juice, was a real favorite with the tennis crowd.”

The star had a close relationship with her mother, Lela.

Rogers loved living with her mother, with whom she’s pictured in the circa 1940s portrait on the piano in this 1954 image. The triple threat pushed back against the term “stage mother” in Architectural Digest; she considered her mom to be “my guide and my professor… she was my encyclopedia. She knew what route to take: She helped Lucille Ball along hers too, you know. It would have been hard to have a career without her.” About their Beverly Hills pad, she added, “we both liked the look of a French farmhouse. And I wanted certain specific things: a helpful bath, a tennis court, and my own projection room, where we had eight or ten director’s chairs, so that friends could come over to watch movies.”

Rogers with a furry friend at home in the 1950s.

The home featured a main house with bedrooms for Rogers and her mom, as well as a guesthouse for visitors. “The house was very bright,” she told Architectural Digest. “I don’t like dark things; even in my clothing, I prefer to be light and colorful—Springtime for Henry has always been my motto,” she explained, referencing the 1934 comedy. In her memoir, Rogers added, “The style was an American farmhouse with Dutch doors opening to cool breezes. The large bay window in the corner of the living room had a view of Beverly Hills and a bit of Los Angeles. Off the living room was a patio for barbecuing on a flagstone area under a beautiful Australian pepper tree. It was a wonderful place to entertain on crisp California nights.”

Rogers’s home also included a solarium, and bedrooms with scenic views. “On a lower level was an outside entrance to the playroom,” the actor noted in her memoir. “This room had big windows and comfortable cushions as did the solarium in the hallway to the patio. I read many a book, with apple in hand, buried in those downy cushions.” About her bedrooms, she added, “There were two bedrooms leading from the solarium, one for Lelee [her mother] with a four-posted bed and one for me. My room looked out on the view of Beverly Hills, and I had a beautiful hand-carved mantel for my fireplace.”

In addition to the stage talents for which she became a star, Rogers was also a painter. Her guesthouse also doubled as a studio. “My studio, which could double as a guesthouse, held all the paraphernalia of my hobbies: painting materials, canvases, paintbrushes, turpentine, pencils, and so on,” she wrote in her memoir. “Whenever there was a lull on set, I’d take out my pencil and sketch,” Rogers added. “I had been drawing for a long time and it seemed to come naturally to me. I found it challenging and relaxing. I never studied drawing or painting, I just did it.”

In her memoir, Rogers recalled a time when she brought her paintings out for a gallery show. “When I’m not working or traveling, my main source of relaxation comes from my painting,” she wrote. “Gallery owners have wanted to have a one-person show of my work, but I never had the time to organize my paintings. Well, now was the time. Gregg Juarez, a gallery owner and friend of mine, arranged for a show and sale at his gallery in Palm Desert. As we were hanging the paintings for display, I realized these were my children—I couldn’t sell them! Gregg told me I had to sell a few so the customers wouldn’t get mad. I managed to put a few up for sale, but couldn’t part with the rest. So now they are joyously hung in my home for all to see.”

Rogers was 83 years old when she died in 1995 at home in California.

Rogers remained at her home on Gilcrest Drive until 1970, when her mom urged her to sell while she was away working in Europe. “I had been renting it out more than living in it lately, and Mother thought it was financially sound to put it on the market,” the actor wrote in her memoir. “Besides, she said it needed a new roof! She handled all the details of the sale…. This was one time I’m not sure Mother knew best. I adored that house on Gilcrest Drive and have regretted selling it ever since.” Rogers died decades later, on April 25, 1995, at her home in Rancho Mirage, per the Los Angeles Times.

#4825. Want Headphones Built for Real Workouts? These 9 Survived Runs, Jumps, and Gym-Bag Chaos

Headphones that can handle as much as you can.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Listening to a hyped-up playlist can make all the difference in your workout. As a fitness writer and longtime distance runner, I’ve seen firsthand how the right headphones can make or break a workout. And I’ve worked my way through a range of workout headphones before I found the ones I don’t want to be without.

I used to constantly fiddle with headphones that didn’t fit right, which is a real motivational buzzkill, and once spent 10 minutes trying to hunt down an earbud that popped out mid-run. (I never recovered it.) I’ve also discovered that some headphones are better for certain types of workouts over others. Case in point: My go-to headphones for strength training at the noisy gym are different from what I reach for when it comes to HIIT and running.

No matter the style and fit you prefer, elements like sweat resistance, battery life, sound quality, and adjustability are crucial, too. And, while I love a good bargain, I’ve learned that you can’t just grab any random pair of cheap headphones or earbuds and expect them to do the job well. After multiple rounds of testing, these are the best wireless workout headphones to consider.

The Apple AirPods Pro have always been a reliable pair of headphones for me, and the latest third generation is even better. Whether I’m biking or struggling through heavy reps, it delivers a premium experience, including impressive sound and a comfortable fit. And the latest edition further proves their God-tier status: heart rate, step, and calorie tracking.

It has a sensor that deciphers your pulse through your ear canals, which then calculates calories burned based on heart rate. I like to keep tabs on my heart rate during high-intensity cardio, so it’s a great alternative to wearing a fitness tracker. Just make sure the fit is right to get an accurate reading (four silicone ear cup sizes are available).

It also has motion sensors that can track your steps. All data transfers to the Apple Health app, so you need to own an iPhone or iPad. Luckily, I recently converted (sorry, Android).

When I’m grinding hard at the gym, I want to hear nothing around me except my hype house music. The active noise cancellation drowns out any grunters, loud gym music, TVs, and general unnecessary background noise. I feel like it’s just me and my music, so that I can laser-focus on the task at hand.

But when I need to maintain awareness during outdoor runs, I turn on transparency mode to hear oncoming traffic and people nearby. I also like that it automatically lowers my music when it detects me talking to someone. It has an IP57 rating, meaning it’s sweat and dust-resistant, and can be submerged in a meter of water for up to 30 minutes in case of any accidental puddle drops (been there). As someone who sweats a lot, each bud repels moisture very well and doesn’t fall out of my ears when jumping or running. Plus, sweat never clogs my ears—something I experienced with regular AirPods. Battery life could be better for all-day wear, but it’s good for workouts (assuming you’re not working out all day). I hit the gym after work, and the power is always drained after an eight-hour day. On the flip side, it’s easy to juice up in 15 minutes with the charging case (it offers up to 30 hours of battery life per charge). To fully restore the battery, make sure to charge overnight. Read More: Best Fitness Trackers

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones are an absolute treasure. I own a lot of headphones, but the sound quality always keeps me coming back for more. The over-ear design completely covers my ears, providing A-grade noise cancellation at prime-time hours.

The sound is immersive with balanced, deep bass that doesn’t feel piercing—an issue with lower-quality headphones I tested. I blast my tunes at full volume when getting in the zone, and I never feel uncomfortable.

They look bulky, but looks can be deceiving. They never budge, even when speed walking at an incline or doing fast-paced plyometric drills. I’ve worn it during box jumps and ice skaters, and it stayed put.

Just note it’s not water resistant for intense cardio like spinning and running, where you’ll work up a sweat—although the plush padding rimming the headband and ear cups can easily be wiped clean.

Like the Apple AirPods Pro 3, I have to charge it daily in the included case, so make sure to keep the cable on hand for quick power-ups.

Read More: The Best Slim Fitness Trackers

If you really just can’t with the possibility of your earbuds falling out, but still want a compact option, Dr. Dre delivered just what you need: the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2. It has hooks that seamlessly glide over the ears, ensuring a proper fit that stays put. And compared to the previous iteration that launched six years ago, it’s now smaller and lighter, and shares many of the same features as the AirPods Pro 3 (Apple does own Beats, after all), including active noise cancellation, transparency mode, and heart rate monitoring through the Beats app.

I’ve put it to the test during long runs, sprints, low-impact biking, and strength training. The verdict? It performs as sleekly as it looks. The sound is crisp and rich, while the bass is heavy without being overbearing.The sweat resistance is a notch below AirPods with an IPX4 rating, meaning it can withstand light rain but can’t be submerged. I’ve gotten caught in the rain one too many times while wearing these—yet, the sound quality is still the same as it was straight out of the box. And battery life is actually slightly better than AirPods, offering up to 45 hours with the charging case.However, this pair feels more uncomfortable than the Apple AirPods Pro 3. The material feels a little too hard for my liking. If you plan on walking or running for hours, the best overall is the way to go.

The last thing you want is uncomfortable headphones when in the midst of PRing your next barbell squat. Working out is tough enough, so having a pair that’s übersoft will take away some of the pain. Meet the Sony WH-1000XM6—a splurge that’s worth the investment.

Thick foam on the ear cups feels like lying on a pillow, while it also seals sound better for superior noise cancellation. The wide headband is plush and fits securely onto the head without being too tight. MH senior gear and commerce editor Ryan Brower throws it in his gym bag whenever he has strength training on deck. He also appreciates the adjustable smooth slider for a custom fit, calling it a fluid mechanism.

The headphones use 12 microphones to isolate and cancel out sound to deliver an immersive listening experience. Vocals and instruments sound balanced and rich, with Brower calling the sound quality superb. Battery life can run for up to 30 hours, while just three minutes of charging can provide three hours—perfect if you’re in a rush to hit the gym.

Brower’s only gripes are the lack of sweat resistance for high-intensity activities, like running or spinning, and that it feels a little bulky. So, he reserves it for less strenuous pursuits.

If you’re into an over-ear design in headphones, you know they can get hot and sweaty fast. But the Skullcandy Crusher 540 headphones feel surprisingly breathable on—for an over-ear headphone. The ear cups are made from a lightweight material that feels breezy against your ears, minimizing extra sweating while you work out.

These headphones also have an impressive battery life of 40 hours, which is only second on our list to the Powerbeats Pro 2. Skullcandy clearly designed these headphones for convenience, with plenty of buttons within easy reach. As a result, you can quickly turn the volume up or down without missing a beat. If active noise cancellation is a must for you, scroll up—while the sound quality on these headphones is excellent, they won’t help you fully tune out the world.

The Skullcandy Crusher 540 headphones don’t have an official IPX rating, but they have a special sweat- and water-resistant nano-coating to protect your gear. (The ear cup pads are also removable for easy cleaning.) A big draw of these headphones is the strong bass, which comes in handy during tough workouts. As someone who loses nearly everything, I appreciate the built-in Tile technology to help you find your headphones with the Tile app if you misplace them.

I first tested the Bose Open Ultra Earbuds last fall, and they’ve been my favorite pair for distance running ever since. These earbuds aren’t going anywhere thanks to a design that’s similar to a clip-on earring. Just gently hook these on your ears and move on. The style is perfect for people like me who have been burned in the past by an earbud falling out and vanishing forever.

As an early morning runner who regularly crosses streets, I appreciate the open-ear audio these earbuds deliver. I can hear my music perfectly, but still can detect things like chirping birds to give me a solid awareness of my surroundings. You can adjust the volume, skip songs, and flip between immersive and stereo sound with a tap on your earbuds, making it easy to switch things up mid-run.

A heads up: If you’ve never used an earbud style like this in the past, you may need to give your ears a little time to build up to wearing them. My ears were a little sore when I first started wearing the Open Ultra Earbuds, but I don’t even feel them when they’re on now. These earbuds are also IPX4 rated for water resistance, so they do just fine with light splashes or rain—just make sure you don't wear these to swim laps.

The earbuds have a seven-hour battery life, which is lower than several others on this list. But I’ve never had an issue with them dying on me. I just pop them in their charging case when they’re not in use.

Some people are going to struggle to get earbuds to fit, no matter what they do. If you have smaller ears and you’re over flipping through different ear tips in hopes something will fit, the Beats Powerbeats Fit are a solid choice. These earbuds actually fit inside your ears like a hearing aid with the help of flexible wingtips that really lock them in there.

These earbuds are small, but they deliver the top-tier sound quality you’ve come to expect from Beats. That includes the options to flip between active noise cancellation and transparency modes, so you can use these to tune out loud gym-goers or to be aware of your surroundings during outdoor workouts.

These earbuds pair seamlessly with Apple and Android phones, making them an equal opportunity headphone. They also have an IPX4 rating for sweat and splash resistance, so you can wear them in the rain, but not to swim laps. While the Powerbeats Fit comes with four different tips, your ears will still need a little time to get used to these before wearing them on, say, a 10-miler.

The earbuds do kind of jam in there, and it can take some time to get used to the feel of the wingtips. But if you’re looking for a discreet pair of headphones that aren’t going anywhere, you can stop your search here.

If you want secure earbuds that aren’t an investment, the Anker Soundcore Sport X20 fits the bill. It costs a third of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 and shares the same ear-hook design that doesn’t budge when pushing your limits during high-impact workouts. The sound is shockingly premium given the $80 price tag. If I were doing a blind test, I’d think it costs at least $200.

The strong noise cancellation blocks out every peep imaginable at the gym. From loud gym music to weights slamming, I can’t hear a thing except my jams. But when I don’t want to be super locked in, I switch to “normal” mode so I can listen to background noise. This mode is handy when running or walking at night. And when things get too wet during intense grinding sessions, the IP67 sweat-resistance saves me. Although I haven’t tested it while swimming, it can withstand water submersion beyond one meter for about 30 minutes.

The silicone ear hooks are soft, flexible, and extremely comfortable. I find myself reaching for it outside of the gym and often forget it’s even on my ears, which I’m not mad about—it makes a great cool-girl accessory. The only downside of wearing it for too long is that the battery will drain after about eight hours. Luckily, the charging case has two days' worth of battery life—so no excuses to skip a workout.

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are my go-to for long-distance running because of the wrap-around and open-ear design that stays in place. It’s no surprise it’s a TikTok-viral favorite among runners and our editors.

The sweat-resistance rating is one notch below our best overall, with an IP55 score, meaning it can withstand intense rain during rough outdoor conditions. Moisture from sweat is never an issue since the design hangs over the ear and doesn’t go in the canal. It even alerts me with a vibrating beep if moisture is present in the port while charging.

If blocking out noise is your priority, you should consider other options, as this pair doesn’t offer noise cancellation. I don’t love that I can’t be fully engaged in my music, but that’s the trade-off for running safely. Unlike other headphones I tested in this guide, the sound emits outside of the eardrum using bone conduction technology, which is when noise is transmitted through vibrations in the skull to reach the ear. I hear every sound, from people talking to traffic, so I give it a perfect score for maintaining awareness. I deem it an essential pair if you train early in the mornings or at night. Just note it’s not going to be the same listening experience as the Apple AirPods Pro 3, for example.

The battery life is nowhere near the capacity of the Apple AirPods Pro 3, with only about 12 hours of playtime, so I find I have to charge it weekly for an hour. The flip side is that it only takes 10 minutes to get two hours of battery life if I quickly need it before a run.

Full disclosure: They come in two sizes, but tend to run large, which is why I went with the mini size. I ordered the standard size first and had to return them (small head probs).

If you plan on running, spinning, or doing other high-intensity training, it’s best to have headphones that can withstand sweat. They should have an IP rating, which is a protection score for how well electronics can resist water. “IPX4 or higher is perfect for working out,” says Joe Smith, an audio specialist at Music Critic. All options on this list have at least an IPX4 rating.

But our best budget option, the Anker Soundcore Sport X20, has an even better score of IP67, meaning it can handle being submerged in just over one meter of water for 30 minutes. If headphones aren’t made to withstand sweat, it’s best to reserve those for lower-intensity workouts.

Having your headphones die during a half-marathon is not the vibe (been there). Using a pair with good battery life is crucial to ensuring the tunes are always going strong during a long workout. With select pairs, it can be dependent on whether or not select features are in use.

For example, the total playtime for the new Apple AirPods Pro 3 from a single charge (with case) is up to 10 hours with active noise cancellation turned off, but only up to eight hours with it turned on. Carl Prouty, a tech expert at Abt, recommends snagging a model that charges fast in case you forget to plug them in the night before.

Noise cancellation is a function that utilizes a microphone hidden inside the earbud or earcup to analyze frequencies that emit opposite sound waves, thus helping to reduce background noise. Blocking out surrounding noise is great for staying focused and immersed, but it’s not the safest feature in desolate areas like quiet trails, busy streets, or at night.

I prefer an open-ear style to maintain awareness during outdoor runs. If you’re not a fan of that design, other options on this list allow you to turn noise cancellation on and off. “If you still want to be able to hear what's going on around you while also listening to music, look for a model with a good ambient and pass-through mode,” says Prouty.

You have a lot to choose from in a workout headphone, and each has its pros and cons. Earbuds rest inside your ears to deliver sound without bulk. These tend to fit comfortably, but may pop out if you don’t get the fit right. Ear hook earbuds add an extra layer—a hook that goes over your ears—to help combat this issue. There are also open-style headphones that hook over your ears and around the back of your head to keep them in place.

A newer category of these is open earbuds that clip over your ear like a clip-on earring, while nestling into your ear like an earbud. Finally, over-ear headphones have soft cups that fit over your ear for a classic look. While these usually do a good job staying in place, they may feel hotter during intense workouts than other designs.

As a distance runner, I rely on good music to keep me hyped up and entertained on long runs. I’ve tested dozens of pairs of wireless headphones for working out over the past decade and learned what features make pairs stand out. Only workout headphones with good sweat resistance, battery life, noise cancellation, and sound transparency made the final cut.

Because everyone has different needs in a workout headphone, I also leaned on experiences from Women’s Health editors, along with Men’s Health senior gear and reviews editor Ryan Brower. Each pair was used in different environments during cardio and strength training sessions to see how they performed when put to the test during workouts. Those included 5- to 10-mile runs, indoor cycling workouts, HIIT sessions, and more general lifting at the gym.

#4823. Iceland’s first wind farm comes with a water-saving bonus

Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.

Vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads. And Iceland’s windiest months coincide with the time of year when less water flows into its reservoirs.

Landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power company, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026. The first 14 turbines are online; another 14 will be installed in a second phase, and the entire wind farm is expected to be operating by the end of 2027.

Once complete, Vaðölduver will have 120 megawatts (MW) of capacity. When I met with the folks at Landsvirkjun in Reykjavik last month, they told me that’s enough to power the equivalent of 90,000 Icelandic households. Vaðalda’s electricity feeds into the grid and is sold through power purchase agreements.

Vaðölduver sits on a lava-and-sand plain east of the Þjórsá River, south of Sultartangi Dam. Landsvirkjun already operates seven hydropower stations in the surrounding Þjórsá and Tungnaá region.

The wind farm was sited in this region of Iceland because the seasons line up nicely.

The winds are strongest in winter, when inflows into hydropower reservoirs can be low. In summer, wind speeds tend to drop, but glacial melt increases water availability for the hydropower system.

When the wind turbines are generating plenty of electricity, Landsvirkjun can ease off hydropower and leave more water in its reservoirs. When the wind drops, hydropower can pick up more of the demand.

That gives the utility more control over when it uses its stored water and helps that water go further.

German wind turbine maker Enercon manufactured Vaðölduver’s turbines. The project also includes a service and maintenance agreement with Enercon.

Landsvirkjun had a decade of experience operating pilot wind turbines before building Vaðölduver. One big thing they learned: They didn’t need tall towers to find plenty of wind.

There’s little vegetation or other surface obstructions across this unique, exposed landscape. That allows the turbines to capture productive winds closer to the ground than they could at a more wooded or sheltered location.

“Lower” is relative, of course. The turbines still reach 150 meters (492 feet) at their highest blade tip.

The wind farm covers 17.1 square kilometers (6.6 square miles). Twenty-five turbines are rated at 4.26 MW each, and the remaining three at 4.5 MW. Landsvirkjun’s presentation puts annual generation at 440 GWh and lists a P50 net efficiency figure of 43%, which is considered strong for onshore wind.

The ability to tap into existing infrastructure was a major factor in Landsvirkjun’s site selection. Where a wind farm goes affects its cost, its environmental footprint, and the people who live nearby.

Landsvirkjun also identifies active engagement with communities and other stakeholders as essential to building wind projects. At Vaðölduver, the immediate task is to finish the remaining 14 turbines while the first phase completes its trial runs.

The company sees wind as a potential third pillar of Iceland’s electricity supply alongside hydropower and geothermal. Vaðölduver shows how those resources can work together, with wind adding generation while helping conserve stored water.

Iceland is a world leader in clean energy. It generates nearly 100% of its electricity from renewable sources, combining hydropower fueled by glacial runoff and rivers (around 70%) and geothermal energy (around 30%).

Over 90% of Icelandic households use direct geothermal hot water for space heating and hot water, while the remaining homes use renewable electricity.

But it’s got the same grid capacity challenges as every other country. Adding wind – and anything else that uses power – means paying close attention to what the grid can handle. Iceland has an isolated transmission system, so maintaining stability and ensuring sufficient capacity are increasingly important as the country develops more projects.

While in Reykjavik, I met with the Minister of the Environment, Energy and Climate, Jóhann Páll Jóhannsson, who told me that the Icelandic grid’s capacity is expected to grow from 20 TWh to 24-25 TWh within a decade. Jóhannsson also said that he is pro-data center and that investors are keen to establish more of them in the country.

When I asked Jóhannsson and his team, as well as the teams at Landsvirkjun and publicly owned ON Power, Iceland’s second-largest electricity generator and largest EV charger network, about grid expansion plans to handle that pipeline, they all said that legislative reforms were being passed to speed up energy permitting processes. There is also financing in place to grow the grid. The physical transmission network is being expanded, but the process is slow because NIMBYism is creating bottlenecks.

In learning about new and completed Icelandic power projects during my visit, it was apparent that the companies in the power and geothermal heat sector regularly collaborate on projects – everyone brings their expertise to the table and works for the common good (yes, really).

But what was striking in discussions about grid expansion was that there seemed to be no plans to pitch in with the Icelandic transmission system operator (TSO), Landsnet hf. It seemed that the plan was to let the TSO come up with the solutions on its own. At most, Jóhannsson’s team said its legislative reform “opened the door” to possible grid innovations.

When I asked the Landsvirkjun team whether they were considering working with the TSO on distributed energy resource (DER) projects like virtual power plants and onsite battery storage for its heavy-industry clients, which make up 80% of its business, they said they hadn’t considered it.

I often wonder why Quebec hasn't followed this strategy. They have huge dams with world-leading power connections, and one of the issue they are facing is a lack of water to refill those dams, due to several years of relative drought. I know it costs a lot to build wind power up north, but siting a project there would re-use their massive investment in power lines. The dams would act as gigantic batteries, because they wouldn't need to drain their reservoirs when the wind is blowing.

Iceland has earned its reputation as a clean energy leader. Bringing that same collaborative and creative approach to expanding its grid would help it keep setting an example for the rest of the world.

#4822. 8 Best Miami Airbnbs to Get You in the Vacation Mindset (2026)

Miami is a hotbed for avant-garde fashion, design, and art, which is why people flock to the tip of the Florida peninsula every year to navigate the crowds at events like the upcoming Art Basel Festival and Design Miami. History buffs can explore architecture from the 1920s at the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens, stroll the Deering Estate house museum, or study up on Miami’s urban and environmental design at the Coral Gables Museum. There’s plenty of nightlife to speak of, too, but if you’re aiming for something more low-key, catch a live performance at the Historic Miracle Theatre, or head over to ArtecHouse Miami to immerse yourself in interactive art.

You could even devote a day or so to scouring the food scene. May we suggest a Cuban food tour of Little Havana or noshing at trendy spots like the playful, pastel-hued Casadonna? Local favorites like the News Cafe, the historic restaurant where Gianni Versace used to venture to pick up his daily newspaper, and newer openings like cocktail bar Little Torch, with its Golden Milk Punch, are not to be overlooked as well.

Just know whether you’re traveling solo or going in with a group, there are countless Miami airbnbs to set you up for an epic trip to remember. The stays we found include a tranquil paradise with a private saltwater pool, a contemporary high-rise condo downtown, and an Art Deco-style suite a stone’s throw from Biscayne Bay. Here, some of our favorite Miami Airbnbs for doing the most (or the least, if relaxation is key) on your visit.

Perks: Wabi-sabi design, zen garden fixture, security system, free parking

Throughout the space, a restrained palette and clean-lined furnishings draw inspiration from Japanese minimalism. A tatami-style dining table, low platform beds, and a concrete bathroom with wood-beamed ceilings make additional ornamentation superfluous. Large picture windows frame the equally tranquil views of the Zen garden just outside. From $648 per night.
