#4762. Bronx Zoo rescues parrots confiscated at the U.S.–Mexico border

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 16, 2026 4:07 PM EST

Over the past 17 months, the Wildlife Conservation Society’s Bronx Zoo in New York City has rescued dozens of parrots from the illegal pet trade. They include white-fronted Amazons (Amazona albifrons) and orange-fronted conures (Eupsittula canicularis).

The United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) confiscated the orange-fronted conures during three separate operations over the last 17 months, and the white-fronted Amazons in the last several months. All of the birds were discovered at the U.S.–Mexico border.

“These animals were stolen from the wild and are victims of the illegal wildlife pet trade, and our responsibility is to give them the best possible chance for a healthy future,” Chuck Cerbini, WCS Bronx Zoo Curator of Ornithology, said in a statement. “Working with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, our veterinary and animal care teams provide specialized expertise to assess, treat, and care for confiscated wildlife.”

When confiscated wildlife arrives at the Bronx Zoo, the veterinary and animal care teams first conduct a health check, provide any necessary medical treatment, and then help find long-term placements for those that can’t be released into the wild.

White-fronted Amazons are native to parts of Mexico and Central America and represent the smallest Amazon parrot. They are also one of the few parrot species in which males and females feature visibly different plumage. Both sexes have a white foreheads, red faces, and yellowish bills, but males have red shoulders and females have green shoulders.

Orange-fronted conures, also known as half-moon conure or Petz’s conure, are also native to parts of Mexico and Central America, where they live in open woodlands, forest edges, and savannas. They have an orange forehead and green and blue feathers.

The IUCN Red List categorizes both birds as a species of Least Concern, but that still  doesn’t justify trafficking them in the illegal pet trade. Parrots throughout Latin America are subject to both the loss of forest habitat and poaching.

Birds in particular l are especially threatened by trafficking because they are valued in the pet trade and the collector trade.

As no-drip, low-noise job sites become more the global rule rather than the exception, Volvo’s incredibly versatile EWR150 Electric wheeled excavators are proving to be a smart addition to construction and municipal fleets – that’s proving true in Luxembourg, as well.

The Volvo EWR150 Electric wheeled excavator is helping the postage stamp nation of Luxembourg connect natural freshwater springs to a planned water reservoir, but the work has to be done in an existing groundwater protection zone, where even the smallest fuel spills or oil leaks could have serious consequences. An ideal opportunity, in other words, for a battery electric machine like the EWR150 Electric to shine.

“Sometimes I miss the sound of the engine,” says Thomas Weber, an operator on the project who’d previously worked with the conventional EWR150 wheeled excavator. “But the quieter operation of the EWR150 Electric is more beneficial for me, personally. Compared to the diesel equivalent, I find the performance and power to be identical.”

Volvo CE took to LinkedIn to share the work being done by the Luxemburgers at construction firm Elenz, touting the Volvo’s clean, quiet running in this highly environment.

For their part, Elenz executives are equally excited about the new machine. “Going electric is not a regulation, but a requirement for this particular job,” explains Christoph Schommer, Managing Director of Elenz. “We are thoroughly impressed by the EWR150 Electric. Its low noise level is a major advantage here. At the same time, the machine offers plenty of power and consistently delivers the same level of energy.”

The EWR150 Electric is built around a 270 kWh, 600V li-ion battery pack powering an electric drive motor that’s backed by a KERS-style hydraulic boom energy-recovery system that works like regenerative braking to extend the machine’s operating time. A 0.67 m³ (~0.9 yd³) bucket with 108.5-kN (~ 24,390 lb.) breakout force is standard, and offers a, 8.95 meter (~29 foot) maximum digging reach and 5.23 meter (~17 foot) digging depth. #4760. Trying to Build Muscle and Lose Fat? Don’t Overlook This Part of Body Recomp

Crushing your workouts is only half the equation.

When it comes to body recomposition, showing up and crushing your workouts is only half the equation. You also need to pay attention to your nutrition to build muscle and lose fat.

And that part of the job isn’t always as straightforward as exercise. In the gym, you know you need to regularly lift enough to challenge your muscles and get your cardio in. In the kitchen, body recomposition typically involves two key things: getting enough protein and managing your calorie intake. As simple as that sounds, it isn’t always easy.

There are a few ways to approach these goals, but one key to making them more sustainable and manageable (and therefore easier to stick to!) is to track your macronutrients, or macros. The three macronutrients are carbohydrates, fats, and protein, and each plays a unique role in your body recomposition journey.

Carbs get a lot of unnecessary hate, but they’re your body’s primary energy source, says Dana White, RD. Your body relies on glucose, a sugar that is broken down from carbs. Without enough of it, your energy, concentration, and mood can all be affected.

Fats are vital to your body’s overall functioning. They support the health of your cells, help your body absorb vitamins like A, D, E, and K, and play a big role in satiety, White says. Protein, perhaps the most obvious of the three, plays a major role in muscle repair and development—important at any time, but especially on a body recomp journey.

Counting your macros can help you stay on track with your body recomposition journey. To find out how much of each macro you need and how to fill your plate, try our Eating for Body Recomp Guide.

Cori Ritchey, C.S.C.S., is the fitness editor at Women's Health, as well as a certified strength and condition coach and group fitness instructor. She’s reported on topics regarding health, nutrition, mental health, fitness, sex, and relationships for several years. You can find more of her work in Men’s Health, HealthCentral, Livestrong, Self, and others.

#4758. In This Seaside Rhode Island Family Home, the Interiors Have an Ever-Changing Color Palette Inspired by the Ocean

“It was like Frankenstein,” says the husband of the shingled postmodern house on Rhode Island’s rocky coast that he shares with his wife and their three young-adult children. Built by his father in the 1980s, the house occupies an extraordinary site overlooking the Atlantic ocean and an expansive marsh. But successive additions had left it architecturally disjointed. The Manhattan-based couple, fresh from updating a Litchfield County weekend retreat with AD PRO Directory designer James “Ford” Huniford, asked him to take another look. “We were thrilled to have him try to rethink this house for us,” says the wife, “which may have been easier in retrospect to just knock down.”

In a favorite sitting room, which Huniford reconfigured from a triangle into a rectangle, rattan Audoux-Minet armchairs and a custom sofa flanked by 1930s Kittinger pedestal tables wear cushions covered in a Colefax and Fowler chintz. The walls, clad in Scalamandré wallpaper, display 1950s ceramic plates from Italy’s Amalfi Coast, while an antique French chandelier hangs overhead. The coffee table is custom and the carpet is from Sacco. “I was impressed with [Ford’s] ability to take risks and do things that were different than he had done,” says the wife, pointing to the chintz fabric, “and we were very happy with the outcome.”

The French wicker barrel chair with a Jasper-covered cushion and a custom sofa, upholstered in Pierre Frey, complete the seating arrangement around a vintage coffee table. Layered beneath are rugs from Doris Leslie Blau and Sacco, the former a midcentury Scandinavian design. Rococo side tables each support a 1930s Camille Tharaud vase lamp, while the 1961 patinated-brass ceiling lights by Jacques Quinet are from Galerie Apaganthe.

Rather than impose a conventional beach-house aesthetic, Huniford sought to evoke the early-20th-century summer houses of New England while preserving the existing structure’s character. His references ranged from the work of architect Fred Lincoln Savage on Maine’s Mount Desert Island to Kilkare, a Victorian oceanfront estate in Wainscott, New York. New rooflines, structural bump-outs, covered porches, traditional divided-light windows, and detailing brought a sense of accumulated history, even as the house was winterized and its systems updated. Expanded interiors and improved flow were achieved with remarkably little change to the overall footprint. “To me,” says Huniford, “the luxury is in the detail of the craft.”

Garden-inspired Ferrick Mason wallpaper enlivens the jewel-box powder room, where a vintage pedestal sink is paired with a Samuel Heath faucet. Antique Italian sconces flank a vintage Italian mirror from Donzella, while a green 1970s pendant by Hans-Agne Jakobsson for Staff and a Rug & Kilim rug complete the space.

In the dining area, English whitewashed painted chairs upholstered in a Pierre Frey fabric surround a custom table draped with an antique coarse-linen buggy blanket and topped with Vallauris woven plates and a 1960s Émile Tessier cachepot. Above hangs a 19th-century Dutch brass chandelier from Brownrigg, while Josef Albers color case studies enliven the walls. “What I love about Ford is: I was like, ‘Are you sure that we should paint the walls yellow?’” the wife recalls of Huniford’s custom paint selection. “And he’s like, ‘I don’t know. This is a whole new world for me, but yeah, I think we should.’”

Inside, the designer took his cues from the wraparound vistas and shifting natural light, particularly during the summer months, when the family spends most of its time here. “The ocean can be dark black and then it can be blue and then it can be green,” says Huniford. “I love the sea. It’s such a magical thing.” That ever-changing palette informed rooms of relaxed refinement, where the mix includes English, French, and early American furnishings, many slipcovered in upholstery washed to achieve an effortlessly lived-in quality. “They don’t like clutter, and they don’t like fussiness,” Huniford notes of his clients. “They like function, and they love form.”

In the kitchen, striped wall covering by Maresca Textiles provides a lively backdrop for vintage opaline globe wall lights, Newport Brass plumbing fixtures, and a collection of vintage ceramics and tableware. A French bobbin chair is from Andrew Spindler Antiques & Design.

In a newly added pantry adjoining the dining area, new and vintage tabletop treasures include Tiffany & Co. salt and pepper mills, a stoneware pitcher by Bennington Potters, green Dieulefit glasses, and bowls from Paula Rubenstein.

The palette of another sitting room takes its cues from the nearby ocean. Braided-rattan lounge chairs by Henry Link, sourced at Brimfield and topped with cushions in a Décors Barbares fabric, flank an armless sofa with Christopher Farr–covered seat cushions and back cushions upholstered in a Fabricut textile. The coffee table, side table, and lamp are vintage; the ceiling fixture is by Schoolhouse, and the carpet is from Stark.

Yet there is plenty of playfulness beneath the restraint. Huniford introduced an unexpected palette and, in a first for both designer and clients, chintz. In the open-plan living, kitchen, and dining areas, where windows were left free of treatments, sea-glass-green doors complement wide-plank walls painted a buttery yellow. Colorful works by Josef Albers, a favorite of the husband and sourced by Huniford, provide a graphic counterpoint near a dining table surrounded by whitewashed chairs and draped with an antique rough-linen buggy cover. In an adjacent sitting room, rattan furniture brightened by cushions in a radiant Colefax & Fowler floral take center stage. “I never thought in a million years that I’d have chintz in my house,” admits the wife, “but it now happens to be my favorite fabric.”

A dreamy layering of florals defines the primary bedroom, from Temple Studio wallpaper and a headboard and bed skirt in Bennison Fabrics textiles to a Matouk bedspread and pillowcases and a blanket from The Company Store. A vase and lamp from Huniford’s vintage stock sit atop a side table from Fernyhough Antiques.

An English neoclassical mahogany desk by Kittinger, sourced on Chairish, is where the husband prefers to work while taking in ocean views. The desk chair and lamp are vintage, while a dhurrie rug from Rug & Kilim anchors the space. The window treatments are fashioned from a Savel textile.

In the primary bath, vintage painted sconces with glass shades illuminate a custom mirror and Grand Brass plumbing fixtures. A series of framed vintage French dried botanical specimens hangs above a vintage blue firkin.

Alan Campbell wallpaper sets the tone in this bedroom, where a vintage bed and console—the latter painted in Benjamin Moore’s Casco Bay—join assorted furnishings from Huniford’s own stock to create a transportive retreat.

In a guest bedroom, twin beds feature headboards covered in a punchy Designtex print and vintage bedding. A side table sourced on Chairish stands beneath a framed collection of 1920s floral prints.

For Huniford, whose primary mission is to understand how all of his clients think and live, the goal here was not to reinvent the family’s lifestyle but to make the house better accommodate it. A windowed banquette in a new bump-out beside the dining table has become a favorite gathering spot; its overhead pottery shelf was inspired by a photograph of decorator and fashion editor Chessy Rayner’s Southampton home. The adjacent sitting room, long a center of family life, was transformed from an awkward triangle into a rectangle, allowing the space to function more comfortably. “Our lifestyle in this house,” the husband now says, “did not change.”

The three-year undertaking benefited from the couple’s willingness to give Huniford considerable creative freedom, and the time to realize his vision. The result feels as though it has evolved over generations rather than been assembled piecemeal, its newfound polish tempered by a familiar sense of ease. “I think a great house should make you feel welcome and welcoming,” says Huniford. And that, it seems, has been the greatest success. As the wife puts it, “Everyone loves to go there.”

Whenever weather permits, the family gathers for meals on the ocean-facing deck, where vintage Brown Jordan chairs with cushions in a Perennials fabric surround a Laurel Group table dressed with a vintage Italian tablecloth, napkins, and tableware.

Huniford’s design extended beyond the architecture and interiors to the surrounding landscape, where the expansive front lawn gave way to meadow grasses, and an asphalt driveway was replaced with gravel. “I’ve done a few gardens for clients before, and I think [these homeowners] understood my sensibility,” says Huniford. “They did not want a lot of maintenance or formal gardens.” The staircase leading to the second-floor entrance ranks among the designer’s favorite structural additions.

#4757. A rare U.S. coin shouldn’t exist. It could auction for $2 million.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 16, 2026 4:45 PM EST

One of the rarest and most coveted coins in United States history is headed for the auction block this week, where it could sell for over $2 million. But while collectors have long dreamed about owning one of the five existing 1885 silver trade dollars, the strange story of their creation remains murky more than 140 years after their minting

The U.S. struck the first trade dollars in 1873 as a way to compete with similar silver coinage in East Asia, but the production was short-lived. Silver market fluctuations and foreign policy shifts led to their demonetization in 1876, and they were only minted for collectors beginning in 1879. By 1884, the U.S. commissioned only 10 trade dollars before finally retiring the series destroying the die casts.

However, a thoroughly corrupt political appointee named A. Loudon Snowden had other plans. Snowden’s career in currencies began in 1857, when his uncle and former Treasurer of Pennsylvania hired the then 22-year-old whippersnapper at the Philadelphia Mint. While at the mint, he pursued various personal profiteering interests, including the clandestine production and selling of thousands of rare coins for collectors.In 1885, Snowden finally retired as Superintendent of the Philadelphia Mint after nearly three decades.

Snowden also gave himself a parting gift before retiring—five 1885 trade dollars that he purchased from the Mint cashier. No one knew of their existence until a year after Snowden’s death in 1912. The first 1885 trade dollar auctioned in 1913 for $1,140 (about $32,174 in current valuation).

Although some numismatists and historians argue Snowden’s five trade dollars were a final grift, other experts argue that the coins have a surprisingly mundane backstory. Until the 1930’s, Mint employees were legally allowed to purchase examples of new coinage for their equivalent amount. Snowden did just this when he previously bought 10 proof 1884 trade dollars, and it’s possible he bought the following year’s coins before the decision not to mint any others. Regardless of the true story, only five 1885 trade dollars exist today—and they’re worth far more than Snowden could ever imagine.

Stack’s Bowers will auction the 1885 trade dollar as part of its Rarities Night series on Tuesday, November 17.

Update 11/18/2026 12:50 p.m. EST: Stack’s Bowers confirmed its 1885 trade dollar sold for just over $1.95 million.

#4756. Should We All Be Seeing a Concierge Doctor?

Paying an out-of-pocket fee could deliver faster, more accessible medical care. What’s the catch?

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

For as long as I can remember, going to my primary care doctor has been simple: I’d schedule an appointment a few weeks (or months) in advance, commute across town for an in-person appointment, and hope that my insurance covered whatever labs were ordered. But lately, many people have been opting for a membership-based system where they pay a monthly or annual fee for on-demand care. This concept is called concierge medicine.

Over the past few years, the number of concierge medicine services like Tia and One Medical has skyrocketed. Between 2018 and 2023, the number of direct primary care and concierge practice sites grew by roughly 83 percent, per a 2025 study in Health Affairs. (But there are also concierge practices specific to gynecology, longevity medicine, and even emergency medicine.)

“Over the course of my career, I've seen a lot of frustrations that patients have had in terms of access to care, long wait times, lack of continuity of care,” says Jane Zhu, MD, a primary care provider and associate professor of medicine at Oregon Health and Science University, and author of the Health Affairs study. There’s a real need for faster, more on-demand medical care—and concierge medicine is one way that patients are getting that.

Membership prices vary, with some costing as little as $9 a month for on-demand urgent and primary care, and others costing as much as $45,000 a year for top-tier care (at-home doctor visits for urgent care, X-ray imaging from your bed, and even private jets on standby for medical evacuation while you’re traveling). If you don’t live in a major city, many of these programs offer telehealth services all over the country.

So, what’s the catch? Ahead, read up on everything you need to know about concierge medicine, including the pros and cons, and who it’s right for.

The premise is simple: paying a membership fee unlocks extra attention and access to care from your doctor.

At most traditional clinics and hospitals, the goal is for doctors to see as many patients a day as possible. (More visits equals more insurance claims and/or copays, which in turn makes money for the practice.) With concierge medicine, doctors don’t operate within this same construct. Instead, they make money from membership fees, which means they can still turn a profit with a much smaller pool of patients. When you schedule an appointment with a concierge doctor, you’re not competing with hundreds of other patients for a time slot in the same way you would for a traditional doctor.

When Kristen Harvey, MD, MPH, a concierge family medicine physician at Mount Sinai, worked in traditional medicine, she only got about 15 to 20 minutes for each patient visit. Now, she has the freedom to extend her visits to 45 to 60 minutes and form closer relationships with her patients. “I'm able to go into deeper discussions from a more holistic perspective and have a different type of conversation,” she says. Talking more in depth about sleep, nutrition, and lifestyle habits in general is key to helping her patients prevent illnesses in the first place—not just treat them when they come up.

Additionally, getting lab work done through concierge medicine may be a smoother process. While some traditional practices may have you drop by LabCorp to get your blood drawn, for example, many concierge practices will just do it on site, and even go beyond your average complete blood count for in-depth lipid, hormone, and genetic panels. But everything isn't always included in the membership, so check before they draw.

When you need a specialist outside of your concierge practice, they’ll often have health navigators—people whose job it is to schedule your appointments for you, facilitate communication between your providers, coordinate prescriptions, and run point on any insurance claims. Because the health care system can feel so fragmented and hard to understand, the health navigation piece is a major highlight for many patients, says Scott Braunstein, MD, an internal and emergency medicine physician and the chief medical officer at Sollis Health, a concierge clinic for urgent and emergency care.

Regarding costs outside of the membership fee and bloodwork, every concierge practice is different. At Tia, for example, preventative care services like yearly physicals or vaccinations are usually covered by insurance, but diagnostic appointments often come with additional out-of-pocket fees. That means that if you come in for a UTI, sick visit, or complaint about a new health problem, it’ll often result in an additional charge on the patient’s end. The average copay for these kinds of visits at Tia is between $15 and $75—not too different from a traditional doctor’s appointment. However, at a high-end program where you pay entirely out of pocket, the care is pretty all-inclusive.

As of now, there isn’t enough data on concierge medicine to determine whether this model provides superior health outcomes for patients—like fewer hospitalizations or better chronic disease management—compared to traditional systems. That being said, there is one undeniable factor that contributes to good health: regularly going to the doctor. A 2026 report by the health policy initiative Milbank Memorial Fund found that people with chronic illnesses who regularly see a primary care provider have lower rates of hospitalization and emergency room visits—and lower health care costs on the whole.

However, in the U.S., about one-third of adults don’t have a usual source of primary care, per the report. Concierge medicine is one way to bridge this gap of primary care access, and give people an easy, on-demand way to take care of their health. Appointments are easier to schedule, can often be taken from your phone or computer, and the experience is designed to just be more enjoyable and convenient. “When we remove barriers for people accessing care, people are more likely to engage in their health. And when people are more likely to engage in their health, they have better health outcomes,” says Natasha Bhuyan, MD, is a primary care provider and the vice president of In-Office Care at One Medical.

If you can get into these models of care, they seem to be beneficial for both the clinician and the patient. But the question remains: “What happens if you can't get into those models of care?” says Dr. Zhu.

The number of clinicians practicing in membership-based clinics grew by 78 percent between 2018 and 2023, per the Health Affairs study. That means that more clinicians are leaving traditional medicine for this model—which could put pressure on an already-stretched-thin primary care system. If more clinicians leave the traditional system, it could become harder for the people who can’t pay for concierge medicine to access the traditional care they need. So while concierge medicine may help some people live healthier lives, it doesn’t yet fix the broader need for more primary care access in the United States, says Dr. Zhu.

The study also found that while concierge medicine providers are growing, the share of physicians actually declined, and the number of advanced practice providers—like nurses, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants—increased. These advanced practice providers were more likely to be new entrants to the workforce with no prior employer. So while there are still concierge providers with a career’s worth of experience, you might be more likely to get a newer provider with less experience if you opt for concierge medicine.

If you’re frustrated with a fragmented health system where you have to be the one to connect the dots between all of your doctors, concierge medicine could be a welcome reprieve. For instance, Dr. Harvey expects to see more and more patients with chronic illnesses opting for concierge models in the next couple of years. If you have a condition like PMOS, for example, you might be seeing five different specialists to deal with the symptoms: a dermatologist, endocrinologist, gynecologist, nutritionist, and a primary care provider.

With a concierge practice that specializes in convenient, wraparound care, you may be able to see multiple of these specialists all in one place, and have a health navigator or coach to help you coordinate appointments, says Dr. Bhuyan. When you’re dealing with complex medical conditions, or just finding yourself going to the doctor a lot for illnesses or infections, paying for extra time and access to your doctor might just make for a better experience.

The term “concierge” can make this form of care seem cost-prohibitive—and some services certainly are. That said, there are a few options with low membership fees that take insurance, including One Medical (starting at $9/month), Sesame Plus ($10.99/month), Tia Signature ($25-a-month membership, only available in some states) and Folx ($44/month).

If you’re using insurance, you’ll have to do your research to determine how much you’ll pay out of pocket. Popular services like Tia, Allara, Folx, and One Medical accept a wide variety of insurance plans, but specify that copays and other fees can vary plan by plan, just like at the regular doctor. If you’re not using insurance, these practices usually specify self-pay costs in addition to the membership fee depending on the visit or service type, and depending on the care you’re looking for, it could be a bargain.

Before committing to a membership anywhere, find out which services will and won’t be covered (like lab testing or imaging), and how easy it is to cancel said membership if you decide it’s not a fit, says Dr. Bhuyan.

A lot of times, you can also find local doctors practicing concierge-style medicine, and there are search tools like MDVIP or NextMD, which connect patients with a network of in-person concierge physicians all over the country. And if you can’t find one near you, there are plenty of large-scale telehealth services at your fingertips. Be sure to research the doctor beforehand to make sure that they’re legit, and that their expertise aligns with your goals, says Dr. Bhuyan.

Overall, health care is shifting more towards patients’ autonomy. They want to “decide how their health care dollars are spent, whether that's through HSA plans or other means. They’re more empowered to choose the service that works for them,” says Dr. Braunstein. So, only you can decide if a concierge doctor is right for you (and your wallet!).

#4753. Shadow welcomes unknown female bald eagle to his nest

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 16, 2026 7:41 PM EST

Internet-famous bald eagle Shadow has endured an up-and-down 2026. From suffering the loss of a clutch of eggs to welcoming two chicks, and from losing his longtime partner to finding a new friend, he’s had a tumultuous year.

After the August death of Jackie, the female eagle he raised chicks with since 2018, Shadow began spending time with a 4-year-old female eagle named Kaydee (formerly KD1). Viewers of the 24/7 livestream of Shadow’s nest could easily spot Kaydee because of her double-banded legs—a silver ring on one leg and a lavender one on the other. The pair appeared chummy as they spent more time together, sharing stick-arranging duties, singing, and exchanging beaky kisses. An unexpected twist arrived this week with the appearance of an unknown female bald eagle spotted in the nest with Shadow.

Cameras spotted the unknown female in the nest in recent weeks, but this was the first time the eagle was joined by Shadow. On Monday afternoon, Shadow landed in the nest quickly followed by the unknown female. The unknown female fiddled the nest sticks while vocalizing and Shadow appeared unbothered by her presence. Eagles will typically defend their nest from intruders so Shadow’s willingness to share his space with an eagle other than Kaydee surprised many viewers.

Shadow returned the nest solo later in the afternoon as the sun set over Big Bear Lake.

As this is nature, all we can do is sit back and see what unfolds. Mating season is approaching, so we have to wait and see if Shadow selects a new partner. Female eagles in Big Bear Valley typically lay their first clutch of eggs in January. Tune in to Friends of Big Bear Valley’s (FOBBV) livestreams to follow the southern California eagles anytime.

Kaydee, formerly known as KD1, is a banded female bald eagle that has been spotted in Big Bear Valley following the death of Shadow’s former partner, Jackie. She was born in 2022, about 70 miles away from Big Bear Lake in the Prado Basin between Anaheim and Riverside, California. Coincidentally, her parents are also named Lucky and Ricky like Jackie’s parents, but they are a different eagle pair.

Kaydee was banded as part of the Orange County Water District’s work to track the eagles born in the area. These bands help biologists track and monitor the birds over time. Kaydee currently has a black spot on her head, but it may not be permanent. It’s possible that not all of her white feathers have come in or it could be tree sap or dirt. She also has two small bands on her legs. One is a small metal band, while the other is a lavender band with “KD1” on it.

Kaydee is almost five years old, so she is just about ready to mate. She was recently spotted on FOBBV’s livestream inspecting the nest and has also been seen hanging out near Shadow. Flying around Big Bear is completely normal behavior for young adult eagles at this time of year.

In January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers who died from cancer in February.

On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.

She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9. Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below six percent, before rising to nine percent. Jackie died early in the morning on August 10. The necropsy did not reveal a single cause of death, and instead pointed to several factors including severe anemia, bird flu, blood clots in her wing and one kidney, and liver and lung abnormalities.

A memorial service was held on September 5 in Fawnskin, California, along with a second celebration of life called Wings Over Big Bear on October 3. The event featured representatives from FOBBV, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, and more.

What Is the Difference Between a Comforter and a Duvet Insert?

A comforter is a single, often quilted, piece of bedding with a fabric cover encasing the doughy fill in between the two fabric layers. A duvet, on the other hand, refers to both the insert and fabric cover. A comforter can be colorful or white, and made in a variety of fabrics. The fabric cover of a comforter is stitched directly onto the fill (down, feathers, or polyester are most common). A duvet’s cover is removable, and often tied to the corners via loops attached to the insert.

Not necessarily. Many duvet inserts are designed to be used on their own, as a comforter, or with a cover. I recommend a cover to help protect your duvet insert, ensure it lasts as long as possible, and make laundry day as easy as possible. Duvet covers act as a protective layer, keeping sweat, body oils, and normal wear from affecting your duvet insert. Plus, duvet covers allow you to add personality to your bedscape, whether you prefer an all-white minimalist look or a maximalist ruffle.

What Is the Best Type of Filling for a Duvet?

Similar to quality, the “best” filling is pretty subjective. People often choose silk, lyocell, down, or down-alternative fills. Down comforters tend to be firmer and heavier, while down-alternatives are usually considered more lightweight and airy. Down-alternatives derive from recycled and allergen-friendly materials, so they’re ideal for people who prefer or require those types of fillings. The fill power will also determine the ultimate comfort level, and most should hover around 650 for a down, cotton candy-like feel.

And again, those care instructions come into play. If you’d rather throw your comforter in the wash, that’s most down comforters in our list can handle it. Meanwhile, some specialty down-alternatives (like bamboo viscose options) need to take a trip to the dry cleaners, which can make them higher maintenance and more expensive long-term.

Does the Quality of a Duvet Insert Matter?

In terms of “quality,” you’ll see the effects in two main areas: the price point and longevity of your duvet insert. For instance, a down comforter with 750 fill power like Brooklinen’s heavyweight comforter is specifically designed for keeping you warm during colder winter months (or for anyone who spends most nights shivering). The fill power makes it lofty and fluffy, but the construction can also keep it lofty and fluffy.

Baffle-box construction, as mentioned above, is also considered a higher quality design option, which holds fill in separate chambers to keep the fill even. All of this said, the most expensive, technically high-quality comforters aren’t necessarily the best for every type of sleeper. And while we love comforters and duvet inserts that run as high as $500, we’ve also scoured the internet and tested alternatives you can shop for less than $100 on Amazon (we’re looking at you, Bedsure Waffle Comforter Set).

It’s also important to keep in mind that your duvet insert’s quality depends on how you care for it. Make sure to carefully read the care instructions, and if needed, take it to a trustworthy dry cleaner for a gentle clean (experts say about two to three times per year).

How Do You Put a Duvet Cover on an Insert or Comforter?

Follow these steps from Monelle Totah, cofounder of Hudson Grace, for a lump-free way to put an insert or comforter inside a duvet cover:

It’s important to always check your specific product’s care instructions before washing. For example, the Buffy Breeze duvet insert recommends a spot clean or dry clean only, while the Boll & Branch comforter is machine washable on a gentle cycle. To take out the guesswork, we’ve included the product’s care instructions right above each of our review descriptions.

Diana Ciechorska, general manager at Park Slope Cleaning, a commercial cleaning company in New York City, says the standard first step for washing your comforter includes treating any visible stains before you load the comforter into the washing machine. “Opt for a gentle cycle with cold water, using a mild detergent,” she says. “An extra rinse cycle ensures no detergent residue remains.”

When taking a comforter out of the dryer, Parima Ijaz, the New Jersey–based founder of bedding line Pure Parima, recommends holding the corners to shake and fluff it. This allows the fill to distribute even after being jumbled up in the dryer. If possible, she says it’s ideal to let the comforter air-dry for an extra day to make sure it is completely dry before dressing your bed.

How Often Should You Wash Your Comforter?

Comforters and duvet inserts accumulate “dust, sweat, and oils, which can cause allergies and wear down the fabric,” says Camden Olivero, COO and cofounder of Clotheslyne, an on-demand pick-up and delivery laundry service. With this in mind, I recommend washing your comforter two to three times a year to help keep allergens at bay and the covering in its best condition (double check the label first, though).

Like your other linens, it’s best to keep your comforter in a cool, dry place to avoid mold or moisture buildup. Keep the comforter out of plastic and cedar too, as these materials can cause yellowing.

If your old comforter is still in good condition, we recommend donating it to charities in your area. However, if you’re looking to purely dispose of old comforters, organizations like Trashie ethically recycle textiles for you to keep them out of landfills—so long as they’re clean and free of soil like motor oil or paint.

What Kind of Duvet Inserts Do Hotels Use?

If you want to mimic your latest hotel stay at home, you’re not alone. We’ve reviewed the best hotel comforters, which are often sold on luxury hotel chain websites like Marriott and Four Seasons. There are several getaways that use Frette’s bedding, too, including The Palace Hotel in Madrid. In most hotel duvet inserts, there are a few common traits: decadent down or hypoallergenic, plant-based down-alternative fills; high fill powers, around 800; organic cotton or bamboo viscose covers for breathability; and carefully designed baffle-box or box-stitch construction to keep fill in place and make it last.

Fortunately, most of our favorite duvet inserts are machine washable and can even go in the dryer. Some will require a commercial washer (especially if they’re bulky), though, and others like the comforters from Quince and Cozy Earth should take a trip to the dry cleaners. Read the care label, and see what’s best for your duvet insert.

Ijaz recommends washing your comforter in a front-loading washing machine since an upright machine is too abrasive. “Using a top loader with a spindle in the middle can damage the comforter and make it harder to properly and evenly wash it,” she says. Otherwise, her general suggestions are like what the experts noted in this story: Wash your comforter on a cold, gentle cycle and avoid harsh softeners and chemicals so the shell and fill stay in the best condition.

How Do I Choose the Right Duvet Insert for Different Seasons?

There are duvet inserts and comforters with heavy fill powers (think 800 and above) for harsh winter months or cold sleepers, lightweight options (400 or below) for summer months or hot sleepers, and medium weights (around 400 to 600) for year-round comfort. We’ve also learned that the fluffiest duvet inserts often give sleepers that Goldilocks-level sleep. “A fluffy, high-loft duvet delivers the most consistent sleep experience across seasons,” Anthony Loiacono, director of rooms at L’Auberge de Sedona, previously told AD. “It provides warmth without weight, and most importantly, adapts to day-to-night temperature shifts.” Frette’s Cortina Medium Down Duvet Filler has all-season appeal, and you can always layer with an extra blanket if you want more coverage on colder nights.

Not all duvet inserts are created equal. This is a lesson you learn early on, when you wake up either sweating or freezing in the middle of the night. The fact is that this annoying experience is also completely avoidable. Reading up on the duvet insert you're considering buying—and actually understanding what all the terms mean—will tell you everything you need to know, including how hot it’s going to be and whether or not the down is going to end up smooshed in one corner come morning. So, I put this guide together with the help of Danielle Trotter, the textiles technical designer at West Elm, to break down what to consider in the confusing world that is duvet insert fillings, fill power, and the different types of construction.

Fill Power: This is the measurement of how much down occupies a cubic inch of space in the insert, a.k.a. how “lofty” it feels. You’ll usually see numbers in the 500s and up. The higher the fill power, the fluffier and warmer it will feel. I typically like fill powers that hover around 800 during the colder months. This fill power is typically on the marshmallowy side of the spectrum and feels cozier and insulating when the temperature outside starts to drop. For the summertime, 600 fill power or so is usually a sweet spot for me since it’s more airy and breathable, but individual preferences may vary.

Corner Loops: If there are corner loops or anchor loops, that means you can use the comforter as a duvet insert. If there are no loops, the comforter might be prone to clumping and bunching within the duvet, so we wouldn’t recommend it unless you have a lot of patience. Some of the loops in this list reach up to 12, which are super helpful to keep the fill even.

Fill Content: Fill material is usually classified as either down or down alternative options.

Outer Shell: The material on the outer shell of your comforter or duvet insert matters. Look at the thread count. I find that fabrics with thread counts around 300 are typically spongy and airy. Consider your preferred sleeping temperature and whether a cotton sateen shell that’s smooth but slightly thicker is a better option than one made of crisp percale cotton. If you’re a hot sleeper, you’ll probably want a cooling material with breathability, like eucalyptus.

Size and Color: The size of your insert is dictated by the size of your bed. Companies usually offer all standard sizes from twin to king, with some brands offering California king as well. In terms of color, white is most popular for the duvet insert, but you can also find ivory relatively easily. Comforter color ranges are more expansive, and you can likely find a hue that fits your decor. I’ve called out what’s available in each of the product picks.

Thread Count: This is the number of horizontal and vertical threads per square inch of the duvet insert's outer fabric. Expert tip: “In theory, people think that the higher the thread count, the better the quality because more yarns are being used,” Trotter says. “However, it’s the quality of the yarns or even the type of weave that really matters!”

Baffle-Box Construction: This design means the comforter or duvet insert has sewn-in square chambers with side walls. “Each chamber has an equal amount of fill, and the side walls prevent the fill from shifting,” says Trotter. “This construction is considered to be of a better quality because warmth is evenly distributed.”

Sewn-Through Construction: This type of construction is when the duvet insert is made of two pieces of fabric sewn around the perimeter, then filled and quilted into squares. This means the top and bottom of the comforter are sewn together. In turn, the fill is shift- and bunch-resistant. While this is a great option for those who like low-maintenance laundry days since you can typically toss these comforter types in the washing machine, the tighter construction usually makes the fill less lofty. Plus, cold air can seep through the seams, so it’s more ideal for a summer bedscape.

#4748. Whale snot helps scientists sequence an entire genome

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 17, 2026 5:00 AM EST

Whale vomit can be turned into expensive perfume. Whale carcasses will sink to the bottom and become marine life habitats. Whale pee nourishes the entire ocean. But how about whale snot? The microbes and other biological material emitted from their blowholes when the giant cetaceans breathe has helped scientists sequence an entire whale genome: Take that whale vomit. The findings are detailed in a study published today in the journal Molecular Ecology Resources.

Whole genomes are crucial for animal conservation. With genomic data, researchers can measure population health, to see how much genetic diversity and inbreeding is present. It can also help identify individual animals for monitoring, help determine an animal’s sex, and estimate the population’s size.

To obtain genetic data from whales, marine biologists historically have had to conduct a skin biopsy. They’ll take a dart, stick it into the whale’s blubber, and take a small sample of the skin and blubber. However, during sampling, boats must get close to the whales, which can disturb them. In some locations and for some endangered species, getting close enough to take a biopsy isn’t permitted or possible.

That’s where whale snot—or blow—comes in. For this study, a team from Scotland’s University of St. Andrews, the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, the North Coast Cetacean Society, and Fisheries and Oceans Canada used several small drones off the coast of British Columbia. The drones were equipped with sterile petri dishes to collect the samples.

The team flew the drone through the exhaled breaths of one North pacific humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae kuzira) at a time, but still sampled several individual whales. The humpbacks generally took one to six breaths every time they surfaced—covering the drone and the dishes in whale snot.

The team collected 58 blow samples from 26 individual humpback whales. They also took repeated samples from the same whales, collected in different encounters and across two years to match the genomes. They then cross-referenced the genomes collected from the whale blow with genomes sequenced from traditional blubber biopsies taken from the same animals.

To keep the DNA from mixing, the team targeted the whale most upwind in the pod, since the blow downwind might mix with the blow from the whales up ahead. Resting whales were never sampled, and the team stopped the drone flights if a whale showed any reaction. More than one third of samples were collected by flying the drone directly from land—no boat required.

The DNA was sequenced to produce two types of genomes. Low-coverage nuclear genomes, which are inherited from both parents, and high-coverage mitochondrial genomes, which are inherited from the mother only.

The team found that the genetic diversity estimated from the blow samples was very similar to the estimates taken from traditional biopsies. Fortunately, the humpback population in the study shows little evidence of recent inbreeding. There is a small proportion of the genome that has long stretches of identical DNA, but the team believes that most likely reflects distant shared ancestry or past population bottlenecks.

According to the team, this research marks one of the first whole genome datasets for a group of North Pacific humpback whales. Previously, only one North Pacific humpback whole genome was publicly available.

“We will use these blow-derived genomes to not only assess population structure and health, but also assess kinship and family ties among humpback whales foraging in northern British Columbia,” Dr. Éadin O’Mahony, a study co-author and marine mammal ecologist who was at the University of St. Andrews at the time of the study, said in a statement. “The aim is to understand how their social bonds form: Are the whales that forage together family, or long-term friends?”

As expected, the North Pacific humpback whales were genetically distinct from their counterparts living in the North Atlantic. This confirms that data taken from whale blow works as well from data taken from conventional biopsies. The drone-captured genetic analyses also correctly determined every whale’s sex, and revealed three previously undescribed mitochondrial DNA variants, which could help show how some of these whales are related. The blow from whales swimming in groups also did not have any sign of contamination from neighboring whales.

About 16 percent of the DNA in each blow sample were also primarily from the microbes living in the whale’s airways. According to the team, this indicates that a single breath could tell us about the individual whale and its respiratory microbiome, opening up a potential new window into cetacean health.

That’s a whole lot of data from just a little bit of snot.

#4745. The Latest Enamel Pieces by Tiffany & Co. Channel Jean Schlumberger’s Dazzling 1960s Icons

Jean Schlumberger didn’t have a background as a gemologist. The Tiffany & Co. designer got his start in the 1930s with costume jewelry, crafting clips, buttons, and other accessories for Elsa Schiaparelli’s couture collections. “The way he came to jewelry was unpretentious: simple coats of paint on metallic works that looked shiny and lacquered,” says Sylvain Cordier, the Paul Mellon curator and head of the department of European art at the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts. “I’mconvinced that starting with costume jewelry very much informed a taste for bold colors.”

A 1960s Jean Schlumberger drawing of a Paillonné enamel bangle for Tiffany & Co.

In the ’60s, at Tiffany, Schlumberger would return to this vivid style in more sophisticated form through the art of paillonné, a process that layers translucent colored enamel on delicate gold or silver leaf, requiring a series of kiln firings. His first paillonné piece, the Croisillon bracelet, debuted in 1962. Philanthropist and Schlumberger devotee Bunny Mellon soon introduced her friend Jackie Kennedy to the style, which the first lady wore so often it became known as the “Jackie bangle.” Schlumberger also applied the enameling to earrings and decorative objects prized by collectors like Mellon, whose Schlumberger collection is held at the Virginia MFA.

Rings from the Enamel by Tiffany collection

Tiffany, which recently announced a collaboration with the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris to preserve Schlumberger’s archives, continues to honor the artistry of his paillonné pieces with its Enamel by Tiffany collection. The house, which employs some of the only remaining artisans skilled in the technique, is expanding these offerings this fall with new pieces that include rings and watches. Despite the decades that have passed since the Croisillon’s debut, Cordier still finds it to be fresh. “When you look at the Schlumberger pieces, there’s this sort of abstract effect,” he says. “I think it’s very modern.”

#4744. Amflow launches its first city e-bikes, packing huge torque and serious smart tech

Amflow has made a name for itself in the electric mountain bike world with its high-performance Avinox-powered machines, but now the company is bringing that same technology to a decidedly more urban environment. The newly unveiled Amflow UE Carbon series marks the brand’s first move into the commuter e-bike market, combining a lightweight carbon fiber frame, powerful mid-drive motor, and a surprisingly long list of smart features designed for everyday riding.

And while these might look like fairly conventional step-through city bikes at first glance, there’s some seriously impressive technology hiding beneath those clean lines.

The new Amflow UE series comes in two versions, the UE Carbon and the higher-end UE Carbon Pro, both built around a full-carbon fiber frame weighing just 2.35 kg (5.2 lb).

The complete bike weighs as little as 20.9 kg (46 lb), which is fairly impressive considering the amount of hardware Amflow has packed into it, including front suspension, a suspension dropper seatpost, integrated lighting, and cargo racks.

Both models use the Avinox M2 mid-drive motor, which delivers up to 125 Nm of torque. That’s an enormous amount of torque for a city bike, and should make short work of steep hills, especially when carrying groceries or other cargo. And to put things into perspective, a lot of city e-bikes have barely 60 Nm for torque, so Amflow is knocking it out of the park for urban power.

A removable 600 Wh battery provides a claimed maximum range of 132 km (82 miles) in the lowest power assist mode, while fast charging can refill the battery in just 2 hours and 23 minutes.

The bikes also feature Avinox’s intelligent traction control system and a new Auto Boost function that automatically provides additional assistance when the system detects demanding conditions, such as accelerating from a stop or climbing a steep hill.

In other words, riders get much of the sophisticated motor technology developed for high-performance electric mountain bikes, but in a package designed for commuting to work or picking up groceries.

The bike is listed as weighing 20.9 kg (46 lb), though that figure conveniently excludes the front and rear racks, mudguards, pedals, kickstand, bike lock, bottle cage, and chainguard. So figure a few extra pounds for all of that gear, and you’re in the right ballpark.

The main difference between the two models is their drivetrain.

The higher-end UE Carbon Pro ($3,899) uses a customized three-speed electronically shifted internally geared hub paired with a Gates carbon belt drive. That should make it particularly appealing to commuters who want a quiet, clean, low-maintenance setup without worrying about chain lubrication or derailleur adjustments.

The more affordable UE Carbon ($3,499) instead uses a 10-speed electronic derailleur developed with TRP.

Both models support automatic shifting, allowing the bike to handle gear changes without requiring the rider to constantly think about them.

Amflow has also gone fairly wild with the technology integration.

There’s a 1.4-inch touchscreen display mounted on the handlebars, a wireless phone charging mount offering 15W wireless charging or 20W USB-C charging, and integrated lighting with automatic low-light activation and brake-sensing functionality.

The bikes even include a hardened steel frame lock on the rear wheel, Apple Find My integration, and a Lost Mode feature that can lock down certain components if the bike is stolen.

Apple Watch connectivity allows riders to check their bike’s status and unlock it, while heart-rate-based assistance can automatically adjust motor output to help riders maintain a target heart rate zone.

Some of these features, like the security and tracking, are immediately effective for nearly all riders, while other high-tech features like the heart rate-based pedal assist can provide even more functionality for niche riders looking to bridge the gap between riding for transportation and riding for fitness.

Of course, all the fancy technology in the world doesn’t mean much if a commuter bike can’t handle everyday errands.

Fortunately, Amflow appears to have taken the practical side seriously.

The bikes feature a low step-through frame, upright riding position, 65 mm suspension fork, and a suspension dropper seatpost offering 125 mm of height adjustment and approximately 30 mm of suspension travel.

The 26×2.0-inch Maxxis tires should also provide a comfortable ride over less-than-perfect city streets.

There’s a front rack rated for 20 kg (44 lb) and a rear rack rated for 27 kg (59.5 lb), with the latter supporting the MIK HD mounting system for compatible accessories, including child seats.

The standard frame is designed to accommodate riders from 155 to 190 cm (5’1” to 6’3”), while a smaller version for riders down to 140 cm (4’7”) is expected in 2027.

I’ve been impressed with the technology coming out of the Avinox ecosystem, and it’s exciting to see that technology finally make its way into a more practical city-focused electric bicycle.

As much as I love high-performance electric mountain bikes, the reality is that most people aren’t spending their mornings bombing down mountain trails. They’re commuting to work, dropping kids off at school, and running errands.

And that’s where electric bicycles can make an even bigger difference.

The Amflow UE series seems to take a refreshingly comprehensive approach to urban riding. The powerful motor is nice, but I’m arguably more interested in the belt drive, integrated security, cargo capacity, automatic shifting, and built-in phone charging.

Those are the kinds of features that can make an electric bicycle genuinely easier to live with every day. And as someone who actually commutes with an e-bike each day as my main form of transportation, these bikes are really speaking to me!

If you ask me, it’s great to see another high-performance e-bike manufacturer recognizing that the future of electric bicycles isn’t just about riding farther and faster on trails. It’s also about making everyday transportation better for the less exciting type of riding, too.

#4743. Coffee could have anti-aging benefits. Here’s why.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 17, 2026 8:55 AM EST

There are a handful of foods and beverages—red wine, eggs, and cooking oils—whose reputations tend to pendulum-swing routinely between “lifesaving” and “death sentence.” I usually hedge my bets by eating these confusing foods in moderation.

The one item I have trouble consuming in moderation might be the most contentious of all: coffee. I am so hopelessly addicted to the stuff that I usually need at least one cup of coffee before going out to meet a friend for coffee.

Despite my unwavering devotion to coffee, the jury is still out on whether my daily fix is actually good for my health. Throughout my lifetime, coffee has variously been purported to protect my heart, disrupt its rhythm, reduce my risk of cancer, and increase it. All I know is it helps me become a fully conscious person every morning. But could my coffee habit actually reduce wrinkles and help me age more gracefully?

A new study conducted at Texas A&M suggests that certain compounds in coffee might protect the body against aging and inflammation.

However, according to Dr. Dung Trinh, the chief medical officer at Healthy Brain Clinic in Long Beach, California, it’s probably too soon to pop open the champagne (or brew a celebratory pot) over the potential perks of your coffee habit.

“It’s far too early to treat coffee—or caffeic acid—as an anti-aging intervention,” Trinh tells Popular Science.

Despite its inconsistent status as a health food, coffee has been consistently linked to longer life and a lower likelihood of certain diseases, though it’s not certain why. The Texas A&M study, led by Dr. Stephen Safe, focused on a cellular receptor called NR4A1.

NR4A1 is a protein that regulates how cells respond to stress and damage. The study found that several compounds in coffee, particularly polyphenols—plant compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties—bind to the NR4A1 receptor. One of these polyphenols, caffeic acid, is found in coffee and many other plants and, despite its name, has nothing to do with caffeine. These compounds seem to promote NR4A1’s protective effects, including mitigating cellular damage and slowing the growth of cancer cell line in laboratory models.

In other words, the harder your NR4A1 proteins are working, the better your cells may be at fending off damage. Sign me up!

After researchers removed NR4A1 from cells in the lab, those benefits stopped, suggesting this receptor may help produce them. So, if coffee really helps NR4A1 do its job, we might just have a new anti-aging drink on our hands.

Interestingly, caffeine does not appear to play a key part in this mechanism, Trinh says. Instead, those benefits seem to come from coffee’s other compounds, like caffeic acid and its fellow polyphenols.

“What stood out to me was that the story was not really about caffeine,” he says. “I also found it interesting that the researchers did more than simply show that these compounds could bind to the receptor—they demonstrated NR4A1-dependent effects in cells. That makes the mechanism more compelling.”

Translation: The study didn’t just show that coffee compounds attach to NR4A1; it showed that this binding actually seems to activate the protein’s protective effects.

Consistent with this, the study also found that decaf coffee demonstrated similar protective effects on the lab cells, providing further evidence that coffee’s benefits may not have anything to do with caffeine at all.

“One of the interesting messages from this paper is that coffee should not be thought of as simply a delivery system for caffeine,” Trinh says. “Caffeic acid, chlorogenic acid, ferulic acid, and several other coffee compounds all interacted with NR4A1, while caffeine showed much more variable NR4A1-related activity.”

So, coffee’s superpower might not come from caffeine at all, at least when it comes to anti-aging benefits.

Before you start guzzling triple lattes in the name of cellular protection, know that “more” does not always mean “better.”

“We simply cannot infer from this study that more coffee means more NR4A1 benefit,” Trinh says. This is because the researchers studied coffee extracts and purified compounds in a lab setting rather than giving human subjects increasing amounts of coffee and measuring NR4A1 activity. Plus, in human biology, it’s possible to have too much of a good thing, Trinh says.

“At some point, additional coffee can bring unwanted effects from caffeine, including sleep disruption, anxiety, palpitations, or increases in blood pressure in susceptible people,” he says. “Those effects could counteract other health benefits. So, this study should not be interpreted as establishing either an optimal number of cups or a dose-response relationship for this pathway.”

Trinh adds that as compelling as the study’s findings are, he doesn’t yet believe they justify changing recommendations around coffee consumption.

Earlier studies have linked coffee drinking to living longer and to better outcomes for some age-related conditions, Trinh says. But those studies couldn’t explain why. This one offers “one possible biological explanation,” he says.

Like most early-stage research, Trinh says, this study can’t be applied to humans sipping their morning “cup of ambition.” Much of the work used a specific cancer cell in the lab, along with mouse immune cells, rather than testing regular human coffee drinkers directly. And while the study identified a potentially promising mechanism, it’s not clear how this mechanism will translate to human health outcomes.

Ultimately, Trinh says, no single food or compound is likely to be the deciding factor in how well we age.

For a coffee addict like myself, though, these findings are the best kind of wake-up call. Coffee may or may not turn back the clock, but it does stop me from hitting snooze 15 times.

“The much bigger determinants of healthy aging remain things such as regular physical activity, good sleep, avoiding smoking, controlling blood pressure and metabolic risk, maintaining social and cognitive engagement, and eating an overall nutritious diet,” Trinh says.

“This study is a promising piece of the scientific puzzle, not a prescription for another cup of coffee.”

#4740. Black bear gets little too close to another bear’s butt and wins award

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 17, 2026 11:11 AM EST

Even Alaska’s bears are not immune from accidentally making things weird or getting a bit too close. Over the summer, rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska watched an odd interaction between two unnamed black bears (Ursus americanus) taking part in Anan Creek’s salmon run.

“Sometimes the bears at Anan share the creek… a little too closely,” the rangers write. “One bear is waiting his turn for a prime fishing spot, and the other is so focused on the fish he doesn’t mind his surroundings. Did the 1st bear make it weird by backing up, or did the 2nd bear make it weird by staying there?”

For this bit of humor, the rangers awarded the unnamed bears with the 2026 You Made it Weird Award.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

The largest national forest in the United States, Tongass covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in the region. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

#4739. A Minimalist House in Italy Makes the Case for Less

The friendship between John Pawson and Noona Smith-Petersen began in New York City in a very 1990s way: working for Calvin Klein. Pawson, then an architectural wunderkind from the United Kingdom, and Smith-Petersen, a young Danish-Italian communications manager for the fashion house, found themselves collaborating on the opening of the brand’s first flagship on Madison Avenue.

Pawson had already earned a reputation for restraint. His earliest residential works (a Mallorca summer house for collectors, an art dealer’s London apartment) provided a series of simple surfaces, plinths, and frames—for objects, for vistas, and for life. The same was true at the Calvin Klein store, where designer and client amplified each other’s design approaches in a meeting of minimalist minds.

Furnished with Hans Wegner chairs and a Pawson-designed table, the dining area opens onto the land thanks to a sliding window wall.

The living area features a table and chairs by Poul Kjærholm.

Pawson’s recent residence for Smith-Petersen and her husband, Enrico Erba Springorum, an Armani executive, makes another case for life with less. “The imprint came from childhood: the minimalism, the Danish design,” explains Smith-Petersen, who grew up outside Copenhagen. “Poul Kjærholm was our neighbor,” she adds, name-checking the widely influential midcentury modernist. There were also formative summers spent at the pared-back house her father designed on the Turkish peninsula of Çeşme. About the location, she recalls, “People said, ‘You guys are crazy!’ But it was a place close to nature and the sea. And then later it became a destination.”

A single sculptural tree dots the courtyard.

An oak bed with integrated bedside tables anchors the primary bedroom.

Ninety minutes south of Milan, the patchwork hills of the Val Luretta are far less isolated. Its proximity to the city has attracted editors, artists, and other creatives in search of space and quiet. That tranquility drew Smith-Petersen to the area when she was seeking land on which to build a compound with her younger brother, Henrik, for their families. (She and her husband have two adult sons.) Over the years, she and Pawson had maintained a friendship. “So when Henrik and I found the property, I had this crazy idea: Why don’t I ask John?” says Smith-Petersen. “My brother said, ‘Forget it!’ But we went to visit John and his team in London and it kicked off from there.”

The primary bath’s bespoke vanity, topped in a Grassi Pietri surface

Smith-Petersen stands in the living area.

A view across the dining table toward the minimalist hearth

The resulting structure, realized with project architect Giulio Marchesi, is the irst of two planned homes on the site, one for each sibling. Sitting long and low on the land, like an ivory piano key dropped onto the hillside, the single-story house frames expansive views of the Val Luretta. “The area of the countryside is so dramatic,” reflects Pawson, whose first visit to the site was in winter fog. “In the summer, it’s very different—it’s so lush.”

At some 2,500 square feet, the house is spacious but intimate, with Pawson’s trademark spareness and remarkable warmth. He designed it along one axis, a long corridor connecting the foyer to the open-plan kitchen, dining area, and living area, then bedrooms beyond. White-painted plaster walls and floors of pale-gray stone, sourced nearby in Vicenza, radiate calm. As Pawson explains, understanding the way the body and the eye move through a space is paramount—and can take time. “You’ve got to learn the choreography,” he says. Living in and feeling the house is key.

The yearslong friendship Pawson and Smith-Petersen had forged helped him understand how she would use the space. There would be mornings at the Pawson-designed table, afternoons on the terrace or under one of the century-old oaks, and evenings making dinner in a kitchen brimming with Scandinavian tableware. In solitude or surrounded by family, there’s complete peace on offer.

“Most architects—contemporaries, colleagues—always say, ‘Oh, it’s impossible, a private house,’ ” says Pawson. The process can be “very emotional. And that’s what makes it good.” Luckily for Smith-Petersen, the primary feeling the house evokes is serenity. “I didn’t expect to be in such awe,” she says. “I was never a country person. Sometimes, I try to arrive a day before anyone else is here and do a silent retreat,” she adds. “It’s where I feel best now. It’s pure joy.”

#4738. The 6 Best Rowing Machines for Your Gym, Tested by Fitness Experts

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WHEN IT COMES to your fitness routine, it can be nice to switch things up. If you don't own one already, an indoor rowing machine is a piece of equipment you can count on for a high-payoff, low-impact (AKA joint-friendly) workout at home. We've got several in the Men's Health gym, and many of our editors have one or even two at home and use them regularly for this very reason. This might be just the total-body workout you've been looking for.

Indoor rowing is an excellent way to improve cardiovascular fitness and muscular endurance. Since it is a low-impact sport, rowing reduces the risk of damage to weight-bearing joints, such as hips, ankles, and knees, which tend to be prone to injury and soreness when doing high-impact sports. But rowing's not just a great joint-friendly form of cardio. A solid rowing workout can also help build strength in more muscle groups than you'd expect.

"The rower is basically the horizontal version of the deadlift and uses similar muscles," says veteran trainer Ian Creighton. "On the drive, the main focus is on the posterior chain—the hamstrings, glutes, calves, and spinal erectors are all being used. In the pull, the quads, forearms, biceps, and lats are used as well."

Indoor rowing machines are a bit more complicated than ordinary home gym equipment, like weight benches or dumbbell sets. Decades ago, they used to be little more than a gliding seat and rope handle attached to a water-filled flywheel. But today’s best rowing machines are a lot more high-tech and sophisticated. That’s to say, shopping for a new rower can be a challenge. We’re here to help with the most important specs, features, and essentials to consider before forking over your hard-earned money. In fact, this piece of home gym equipment is an industry standard used by CrossFit and many high-profile competitions. The RowErg has a durable construction that can support people up to 500 pounds. Our editors have used the RowErg in their home gyms for years and found it still works like new. It's easy to assemble, too. In our experience setting up this rower, it takes about 15 minutes, ideally with two people, and minimal tools or hardware (just eight screws). I set mine up myself with no issue, and it took no longer than 10 minutes. Not trying to brag or anything, but it was easy. (I posted a video about the assembly here). Plus, it separates into two pieces for easy storage, making it a great option for people with smaller home gym setups.

Yes, it lacks smart connectivity and the big, beautiful LED screens found in newer models like the Hydrow, but if you're looking for a tough-as-nails machine that can keep up with your toughest workouts, the RowErg delivers the definitive home rowing experience.
